pangeos-terayacht.mechanism: However large, a vessel at sea is governed by the law of the country whose flag it flies. Pangeos would therefore be a very big ship under one state's law, and it would create no new territory.
pangeos-terayacht.story:
Pangeos is a design for a floating city shaped like a giant turtle. It was published in 2022 by Lazzarini, a design studio, which calls it a terayacht, a word coined for vessels larger than superyachts, megayachts and gigayachts. It has no owner, no builder and no hull. It appears here because it shows what would happen, in law, to the largest floating home anyone has yet drawn.

The figures come from the designers. Pangeos would be 550 metres (1,800 feet) long and 610 metres (2,000 feet) wide, which would make it the largest floating structure ever built, at a stated cost of $8 billion. The city would be laid out in blocks around a port and a main square, with hotels, shopping malls, apartment blocks and parks. Smaller ships could dock in the port and aircraft could land on an upper shell surrounded by gardens. Underneath, 30,000 cells would keep it afloat above a steel base, and it would sit 30 metres deep in the water. Solar panels on the roof would supply power, along with wings meant to draw energy from the drag and the waves. Its top speed would be five knots, about 9 kilometres an hour, and it would have no fixed route or home port.

No shipyard is big enough to build it. The designers propose dredging around one square kilometre of sea and building a circular dam to make a construction site, and they have named King Abdullah Port in Saudi Arabia, 81 miles north of Jeddah. They hoped to start in 2033 and take eight years. To raise money they run a crowdfunding scheme selling virtual entrance tickets for $16 and virtual VIP apartments for $169 as NFTs, which are digital records of ownership. A buyer gets a virtual apartment, and the money can count towards a deposit on a real one if the real one is ever built.

The law does not change with size. At sea, a vessel is governed by the country whose flag it flies, meaning the country where it is registered. Pangeos would need such a registration before it could sail, and residents would live under that country's law. Moving slowly and having no home port would not make it a territory. CNN's 2022 report names no flag, and none is known. Nothing has been built, and the $8 billion has not been shown to exist.

radio-caroline.mechanism: Britain could not reach a ship broadcasting from international waters, so it made rules for its own subjects. Banning them from supplying or advertising on the station avoided any decision about who governed the vessel, until a 1990 law allowed boarding as well.
radio-caroline.story:
Radio Caroline was a radio station that broadcast pop music to Britain from ships anchored in the North Sea, just outside British waters. In 1964 the only way to hear pop on the radio in Britain was limited. The BBC held a monopoly on British radio, and the General Post Office licensed everything else, including the wireless. The one rival, Radio Luxembourg, broadcast from abroad and promoted sponsored programmes paid for by the four big record labels.

Ronan O'Rahilly, an Irish businessman who managed musicians, could not get his singer Georgie Fame played on the BBC or on Luxembourg. He bought a former Danish ferry in February 1964. It was fitted out at Greenore in Ireland, a port his father owned, renamed MV Caroline and registered in Panama. Next to it, Allan Crawford was converting a second ship, MV Mi Amigo, for his own station, Radio Atlanta. It left Greenore on 23 March for a supposed destination in Spain and anchored off Felixstowe in Suffolk instead. Regular programmes began at noon on 28 March 1964.

The idea rested on a simple legal gap. A country's law over radio ran only as far as its territory and the sea beside it, which for Britain then meant three miles. A foreign-registered ship beyond that line needed no British licence. Caroline's daytime audience reached about 7 million, mostly aimed at housewives at first, and advertising paid the bills. In July 1964 Caroline and Atlanta merged. The Mi Amigo became Radio Caroline South off Frinton-on-Sea in Essex, and the Caroline sailed north to become Radio Caroline North. DJs and crew lived aboard, and small supply boats called tenders brought people, food and fuel from shore.

Governments complained that the ships interfered with emergency shipping channels and foreign stations, paid no royalties to musicians and used wavelengths in breach of international agreements. Their answer was a European treaty of 1965, the Agreement for the Prevention of Broadcasts Transmitted from Stations outside National Territories. Britain applied it in the Marine, &c., Broadcasting (Offences) Act 1967, in force from 15 August 1967. The Act did not attempt to seize the ships. It made it a crime for anyone under British law to supply them, carry goods or people to them or advertise on them. Most British offshore stations closed. Six weeks later the BBC started Radio 1, modelled largely on the pirate Radio London.

Caroline stayed on air and moved its supply operation to the Netherlands, which did not ban such stations until 1974. That worked until March 1968, when a Dutch salvage firm towed both ships to Amsterdam over unpaid servicing bills. The Mi Amigo returned to the air in 1972, supplied in secret, and some boat owners were prosecuted. It sank in a storm on 20 March 1980.

A larger ship, the former trawler MV Ross Revenge, took over in August 1983. Britain moved its sea limit from 3 to 12 miles in 1987, so the ship had to anchor further out in rougher water. In August 1989 Dutch officials boarded it, arrested Dutch nationals and removed most of the broadcasting gear. They argued that its Panamanian registration had lapsed in 1987 and that it therefore had no flag state to protect it. In 1990 Britain changed its law to allow boarding foreign ships in international waters if their signal could be received in Britain. Lack of fuel and supplies stopped broadcasts on 5 November 1990, and in November 1991 the ship drifted onto the Goodwin Sands.

Volunteers kept the ship afterwards. The station went on by satellite and internet, and in May 2017 Ofcom, the UK broadcasting regulator, gave it a community licence for Suffolk and north Essex. Full-time broadcasts on 648 kHz began on 22 December 2017. The 27 years at sea show what a state does when it cannot lawfully reach a ship. It cuts the links to land, including advertisers, suppliers and staff, and it asks whether the ship's own registration is valid.

radio-mercur.mechanism: Denmark had no power over a ship in international waters, so it made the work on land illegal. Recording programmes or supplying the ship from Danish soil became an offence, which ended the station.
radio-mercur.story:
Radio Mercur was a pop music station that broadcast to Denmark from a ship in international waters from 1958 to 1962. It was probably the first commercial radio station anywhere to work from an anchored ship. Denmark's radio then belonged to one state broadcaster, Statsradiofonien, and no one else could legally go on air.

In summer 1958 Peer Jansen, a 27-year-old office trainee, and his cousin Børge Agerskov, a law student, had grown tired of the conservative music on state radio. They wanted a station paid for entirely by advertising. Agerskov noticed a gap. Radio in international waters was regulated only by international agreements, and those had not imagined a ship broadcasting regularly from anchor. The idea came partly from Radio Luxembourg and from Voice of America, which broadcast from a US Coast Guard vessel in the Mediterranean. The millionaire silver trader Ib Fogh supplied the money, and the staff they gathered were mostly people with no radio experience.

Regular broadcasts began on 2 August 1958 from the ship Cheeta Mercur in the Øresund, the strait between Denmark and Sweden. Day to day, the ship did little except transmit. All programmes were recorded in studios in Copenhagen, and the tapes were taken out by boat. Later a larger ship, Cheeta II, lay in the Great Belt, between the Danish islands of Zealand and Funen, so that the signal covered most of Denmark. The station changed frequency more than once in response to complaints from the Danish authorities. A Swedish station, Skånes Radio Mercur, began on the same ship that December. Former staff started a rival, DCR, in September 1961, and the two merged in January 1962.

Danish newspapers called it a pirate and printed cartoons of it with pirate symbols. At first the government had no legal means to stop it. In June 1962 the Danish parliament passed a bill banning all participation in supporting such broadcasts, including recording them, from 1 August. Sweden and other Nordic countries passed similar laws at the same time. The law did not need to touch the ship, because the studios, the staff and the money were all on land. Radio Mercur closed officially on 31 July 1962, with a last three days of broadcasts from 13 to 15 August.

Its success led directly to Radio Veronica, Radio Nord and others. The name came back as a station in Majorca in 1969 and 1970, on the Spanish Costa del Sol from 1982 to 1984, and as a legal local station in Copenhagen from 1987 to 1994.

radio-nord.mechanism: A state cannot board a foreign-registered ship in open water, but it can act on what touches its own territory. Sweden used a power of seizure at port, pressure on the flag country and a ban on selling the station's advertising.
radio-nord.story:
Radio Nord was a Swedish-language pop station broadcast from a ship anchored in international waters of the Baltic Sea off Stockholm, from 8 March 1961 to 30 June 1962. Newspapers called it a pirate, but it worked within the laws of the time, and its offices were openly in central Stockholm. A company formed by Texas broadcasting and political figures owned it, among them the broadcaster Gordon McLendon and the investor Clint Murchison Jr. McLendon's American radio style shaped the sound, with Top 40 music, jingles and advertisements, many for products linked to American companies.

The practical work of getting it on air shows how much such a station depended on the land. The ship began as MV Olga. Its hold was converted into studios, a transmitter room and crew quarters at a shipyard in Hamburg in 1960. German law restricted installing unlicensed broadcasting gear at the port, so the ship, now called Bon Jour, moved to the free port at Copenhagen, where the mast and the transmitters were fitted. The transmitters had been flown from Dallas in thousands of parts. Technical faults and a storm sent it back to a Stockholm shipyard several times in early 1961. It reached its anchorage on 1 March.

The next day, 2 March 1961, the Swedish parliament passed laws allowing officials to seize the broadcasting equipment if the ship entered a Swedish port again. Sweden also pressed Nicaragua, where the ship was registered, to withdraw the registration. A ship's registration is what gives it a flag and a country's law, so this attacked the ship's legal standing. The owners renamed it Magda Maria and registered it in Panama. In December 1961 a storm broke its anchor and it put into the Swedish port of Sandhamn. The new law was not applied, because it had come in under emergency to save the ship.

Sweden's last step was a law against selling advertising on the station, which was the part of the business that had to touch land. Radio Nord closed at the end of June 1962, one month before that law took effect, and ended with a montage of its jingles. The station had been heard in Sweden, southern Finland and parts of eastern Europe.

On 4 July the ship sailed for Ferrol in Spain and was renamed Mi Amigo. In 1964 it appeared off Essex as Radio Atlanta and then Radio Caroline South. Sweden had shut the station without ever boarding the ship, and the same hull went on broadcasting off another country's coast. In March 2011 Sweden's telecoms regulator approved a temporary station to mark the 50th anniversary.

radio-veronica.mechanism: A government can tolerate a station at sea for years and then close it by law on land. The Dutch ended Veronica after 14 years by banning anyone from supplying offshore stations from shore.
radio-veronica.story:
Radio Veronica was a Dutch pop station broadcast from a ship off the coast of the Netherlands from 1960 to 1974. Dutch radio was then made by state-licensed organisations based in the town of Hilversum. A group of independent retailers of radios, televisions and household appliances set up Veronica for a commercial reason, to sell more radio sets by giving people something else to listen to. It first called itself VRON, short for Free Radio Station Netherlands, and later took its name from a children's poem by Annie M. G. Schmidt.

Regular broadcasts began on 6 May 1960 from a former lightship, the Borkum Riff, anchored off the Dutch coast with a one-kilowatt transmitter. The ship mainly transmitted. Most programmes were recorded at a studio in Hilversum, the same town as the official broadcasters, and taken out to it. Advertisers were reluctant at first, but those who bought time reported more sales, and income grew. Veronica became the most popular station in the country. In August 1964 it bought a converted trawler, MV Norderney, with a 10-kilowatt transmitter, and the Borkum Riff was sold for scrap.

The government's first move was against someone else. In 1964 a commercial radio and TV station began from REM Island, a steel platform fixed to the seabed about 10 kilometres off Noordwijk. Parliament passed a law on 12 December 1964 that divided up the North Sea seabed and placed the platform under Dutch law, and marines boarded it five days later. That law worked on a structure attached to the seabed. A ship at anchor was a different matter, and the government also left Veronica alone because of its popularity.

The station's end came from a rivalry. In 1970 Radio North Sea International, on the Swiss ship Mebo II, anchored a mile away with a far stronger transmitter. Veronica paid it 1 million guilders to go silent for two months and put its own crew aboard, and the deal collapsed in January 1971. Veronica sued and lost. On 15 May 1971 three men in a rubber dinghy set the Mebo II on fire. Veronica's advertising director, Norbert Jurgens, and its director, Bull Verweij, were arrested. Verweij said on television that he had paid a man to tow the rival into Dutch waters so that it would be seized. All five people convicted received a year in prison.

That gave the government its reason to draw up a ban. Veronica campaigned against it and planned a rally in The Hague for 18 April 1973. On 2 April the Norderney lost its anchor in a storm and ran aground on Scheveningen beach. Radio Caroline's ship carried Veronica's programmes from 11 April, and the Norderney was back at sea on 18 April. The law passed anyway, banning supply of such stations from shore from 1 September 1974. Veronica closed at 6 pm on 31 August 1974.

Some of its staff then applied for a licence. They were given one and opened a state network, Hilversum 4, in December 1975. In 1995 Veronica left the public system to run commercially, and the name lives on in Dutch broadcasting. The case shows a state choosing how long to tolerate something it could stop, and acting once public support weakened.

rni-mebo-ii.mechanism: States could not board a foreign-owned ship in open water, so they acted from outside it. Britain jammed its signal, and the Netherlands later cut off its supplies from shore.
rni-mebo-ii.story:
Radio North Sea International (RNI) was a pop station run from the ship Mebo II off the coasts of the Netherlands and Britain from 1970 to 1974. Its owners were two Swiss engineers, Edwin Bollier and Erwin Meister, whose firm was called Mebo Telecommunications. In 1968 they had been part of another offshore project, Radio Gloria, which fell apart when West Germany banned offshore broadcasting. So they bought their own ships.

In 1969 they bought the Silvretta, a 630-tonne vessel 53 metres long, built in the Netherlands in 1948, and painted it in psychedelic colours. It carried a 105-kilowatt medium-wave transmitter, the strongest on any pirate ship, though it usually ran at 60 kilowatts or less, along with shortwave and FM. A small boat, the Trip Tender, took out supplies. Regular broadcasts began on 11 February 1970 in English and German. In March the ship moved to international waters five miles from Clacton in Essex.

Britain had already banned its own people from helping such stations, but this ship was Swiss-run and supplied from abroad. So from 15 April 1970 the Labour government jammed it, which means sending out a noise on the same frequency so that listeners hear interference. When RNI changed frequency the jamming followed, and it also disturbed BBC Radio One in Kent. Five days before the election of 18 June 1970, the station renamed itself Radio Caroline International and told listeners that a Labour win would close it and that they should vote Conservative. The Conservatives won, but the jamming continued, and the ship went back to the Dutch coast in July.

The next threats came from business rivals and not from any government. On 29 August 1970 a salvage tug came alongside with Kees Manders, a nightclub owner linked to Radio Veronica, who had a dispute with the owners over a directorship. The crew refused to let others aboard and asked for help on air, and they armed themselves with knives and petrol bombs. RNI then closed on 24 September in return for 1 million guilders from Veronica, which wanted it off the air. When the two months ended, Bollier tried to return the money, Veronica refused, and on 5 January 1971 he went aboard and took command. RNI was back on the air by February. Veronica sued and lost.

On the night of 15 May 1971 a bomb thrown from a dinghy set the bridge and engine room on fire, and RNI sent mayday calls on air. Everyone was rescued, and the station was broadcasting again the next morning. A Veronica director said on Dutch television that he had paid a man 12,000 guilders to force the ship into Dutch waters, inside the three-mile limit, where it could be seized. All five people convicted received a year in prison, even though Bollier and Meister did not want to prosecute.

The case shows the weak point of being out of reach of the law. Nobody protects the ship, and its only remedy is to go ashore and use a court. The attack also persuaded the Dutch government to ban supplying offshore stations from the mainland, in force from 1 September 1974, and RNI closed on 31 August. Libya bought both ships in early 1977, and they reached Tripoli on 9 February. Mebo II was renamed El Fatah and broadcast for Libya. The two ships were reportedly later used by the Libyan navy for target practice and sunk in the Gulf of Sidra.

sea-shepherd-piracy.mechanism: In 2013 a US appeal court read 'private ends' in the international definition of piracy to include goals beyond money. Under that ruling, attacks by private ships on the high seas can count as piracy even when activists carry them out for a cause.
sea-shepherd-piracy.story:
Sea Shepherd Conservation Society is an environmental group that uses ships to confront whalers and other fishing vessels. Its founder, Paul Watson, left Greenpeace in 1977 after being voted off its board over his confrontational methods, and his group's first action was against Canadian seal hunting in 1979. It matters here because of a court ruling. A US appeal court decided that a group acting for a cause on the open sea, under no government's authority, could count as pirates, and that matters to anyone who thinks the high seas are a place with no law.

The conflict was in the Southern Ocean, around Antarctica. Japanese researchers, the Institute of Cetacean Research and others, hunted whales there under a research permit issued by Japan. The 1946 International Convention for the Regulation of Whaling lets a member state issue such permits. Sea Shepherd regarded the hunt as illegal and went after the fleet year after year. In 2014 the International Court of Justice separately ruled that Japan's programme was not for scientific purposes.

The whalers sued in the United States under the Alien Tort Statute. This old US law lets foreigners bring claims in US courts for wrongs done in breach of the law of nations or a US treaty. They asked for an order to stop the attacks. Their main claim used the definition of piracy in the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the main treaty on ocean law. It defines piracy as illegal violence on the high seas committed for private ends by the crew of a private ship against another ship. The trial judge dismissed the claim, reading private ends to mean financial gain and reasoning that attacking ships and equipment was not violence against people.

On 25 February 2013 the US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit reversed that decision. Chief Judge Kozinski opened with the words 'You don't need a peg leg or an eye patch.' He listed ramming ships, throwing glass containers of acid, dragging metal-reinforced ropes to damage propellers and rudders, firing smoke bombs and flares with hooks, and pointing high-powered lasers at other ships. The court said private is normally the opposite of public, and that acts for private ends in piracy law are those not done on behalf of a state. A person's purpose, however idealistic, did not change that. It also held that the treaty covers violence against ships and property.

The ruling applies to courts in one part of the United States and does not bind other countries. The court later held Sea Shepherd in contempt over attacks by its foreign affiliates, and in 2015 the group agreed to pay $2.55 million. A settlement announced on 23 August 2016 permanently barred it and Watson from attacking the whalers or coming within 500 yards of their ships on the open sea.

Watson was removed from the board of Sea Shepherd Global in late 2022 and started a separate organisation. He was arrested in Greenland in July 2024 on a Japanese warrant and freed on 17 December 2024 after Denmark rejected extradition. For a person planning to act at sea outside any state, the lesson is direct. Lacking a government's authority does not free a ship from the law, because that lack is part of what the piracy rule describes. A court in a country where the group has assets or offices can then enforce the result on land.

ss-rex-gambling-ships.mechanism: A coastal state's waters are measured from a legal line, and where that line crosses a bay can decide whether a ship is inside them. California also claimed it could stop a nuisance beyond its waters, and federal law later banned gambling ships in US waters outright.
ss-rex-gambling-ships.story:
The SS Rex was a floating casino anchored in Santa Monica Bay, off Los Angeles, in 1938 and 1939. Gambling was illegal in California. The state's power stopped three miles from the coast, however, and federal law did not forbid gambling at sea. Starting in 1928, operators anchored ships just outside the three-mile line and ferried customers out from the shore. By 1930 there was a small fleet of them. Local officials tried to shut them down many times, and the operators mostly won in court. The early barges Monfalcone and Johanna Smith were both lost to fire.

Tony Cornero, who had gone to prison for breaking the laws against alcohol during Prohibition, launched the Rex in 1938. It aimed at middle-class customers with free or cheap food and transport, and he publicly offered $100,000 cash to anyone who could find a rigged game. It ran day and night with 1,000 to 3,000 gamblers aboard at any one time. It had no engines, so it stayed where it was anchored.

Within months the Los Angeles District Attorney, Buron Fitts, took over water taxis and sailed out with the sheriff to arrest Cornero, who submitted so that he could fight the point in court. The case turned on where the coast legally is. Three miles from the coast sounds simple, but a bay complicates it, because the water inside a true bay counts as inland. Fitts argued that Santa Monica Bay was inland water, so the three miles should be measured from a line drawn between Point Vicente and Point Dume. That would put the Rex inside California and force any ship many miles further out. Cornero answered that it was only a bight, an open curve in the coastline, so the three miles ran from the shore. Fitts won at first, and the ruling was overturned on appeal.

In 1939 California Attorney General Earl Warren tried a different argument. He called the ships a great nuisance and said that a state can stop a nuisance even when it lies outside its jurisdiction. On 1 August 1939 state authorities raided the Texas and the Rex off Santa Monica and the Showboat and the Tango off Long Beach. The Rex gated off its landing platform and turned fire hoses on the police boats. Warren knew that a ship with no engines could not leave, and he waited. After eight days Cornero surrendered, saying he needed a haircut. A court ruling later that year shut the ships for good.

Cornero tried again in 1946 with the SS Lux off Long Beach, which was quickly closed. In 1948 President Truman signed a federal act banning gambling ships in US waters. In 1982 the international limit of a country's waters moved to 12 nautical miles, which made anchoring just outside far more costly. The Rex shows two limits of a legal gap. A line on the water depends on how lawyers measure it, and a business that needs customers to reach it from shore every day can be starved by whoever controls the shore.

villa-vie-odyssey.mechanism: A residential ship keeps people away from any one country's daily control, but it still needs a flag state (the country whose registry and law it sails under), repair yards and permission from each port it enters.
villa-vie-odyssey.why: Sources disagree on the chief executive: Cruise Hive names Kathy Villalba as CEO in the 26 October notice, while Cruise Industry News, citing CBS, names Mikael Petterson. The entry keeps Petterson.

villa-vie-odyssey.story:
The Villa Vie Odyssey was a former cruise ship turned into a permanent floating home. Residents bought cabins and sailed around the world for years at a time. The company, Villa Vie Residences, announced in December 2023 that it was taking over the Braemar from the cruise line Fred Olsen. It sold cabins, called villas, from $99,999 plus a monthly fee, for the working life of the ship, which it put at 15 years or more. It aimed its sales at adventurous retirees and people who work online while travelling, and the first voyage was planned to reach 425 ports in 147 countries.

The idea appeals to people who want to live without staying in any one country. In practice a home like this is a business, and it depends on steel, fuel and ports. The ship was about 30 years old and had been out of service for four years. It was due to start in May 2024. In summer 2024 it sat for months at the Harland & Wolff repair yard in Belfast while the company worked on rudder shafts, steel and engines. It finally sailed on 30 September 2024.

A year later a company press release claimed 46 countries, 138 ports and hundreds of full-time residents. It offered ownership from $129,999 and a lifetime plan from $99,999 called the Golden Passport, which is the name of a cruise plan and is not a travel document of any state. Residents remained citizens of their own countries and needed permission to enter each port. A resident, Randy Cassingham, estimated that the ship peaked at around 350 residents, against a capacity of about 650, with roughly 200 active at the end. He understood that about 85 percent of cabins had been sold, but many were unoccupied, and monthly fees had not started on those. So the company had sold cabins and yet was collecting less of the running income than the sales figure suggests.

The money ran out at sea. Chief executive Mikael Petterson blamed fuel, saying the company had paid about $700 a ton before the war with Iran began in late February 2026 and $2,000 to $3,000 a ton since. The company said monthly fuel costs had risen from about $1,800 per cabin to $6,000 to $8,000 per cabin in parts of Asia. It did not pass that on to residents. It slowed the itinerary to five or six days in each port and borrowed to meet payroll. Residents reported cancelled port calls and reduced food service. Cassingham said crew pay had fallen behind, and he described problems beyond fuel, including the business model and management mistakes.

On 26 October 2026, at Sihanoukville in Cambodia, residents were told they had until 2 pm that day to leave with their belongings because the company could not secure fuel. More than 200 people, mostly Americans, went ashore. The company spoke of restructuring, and Petterson told CBS News it planned to file for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, a US process that lets a company keep operating while it reorganises its debts. No filing had been reported by 29 October. Cassingham disputed the company's claim that it was covering residents' lodging.

The company never claimed to be a sovereign territory, and no government challenged it. It is included because it tested the simplest version of living outside any one country, and it shows who carries the risk. A resident holds a contract with a company, and when the company fails, the resident becomes a creditor in a bankruptcy and has to find housing in whichever country the ship stopped.

women-on-waves.mechanism: A ship registered in one country carries that country's law onto the high seas. In Women on Waves v Portugal (2009) the European Court of Human Rights limited how far a coastal state may go to keep such a ship out.
women-on-waves.story:
Women on Waves is a Dutch non-profit group, created in 1999 by the doctor Rebecca Gomperts, that sails to countries with strict abortion laws and takes women out to international waters to give them abortion pills. Gomperts, born in 1966, had worked as a doctor on the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior II, and what she saw of illegal abortion on its visits to Latin America led to the idea. The group claims no territory of its own. It relies on a rule of the sea that applies to every ship, and it shows how far that rule goes.

The rule works like this. A country's criminal law generally stops at the edge of its territorial sea, the belt of water reaching 12 nautical miles from the coast. Beyond it, on the high seas, a ship follows the law of its flag state, the country where it is registered. So once a Dutch-registered ship is out at sea, Dutch law applies on board, including the Dutch law allowing abortion. Women make appointments in port, are taken on board, are given the pills in international waters and then come back.

The clinic itself is a shipping container, called the A-Portable, designed by the Dutch studio Atelier van Lieshout. It is strapped to a rented Dutch-registered ship and normally staffed by two doctors and a nurse, with volunteers who give education and counselling. In 2002, after a contested debate in the Dutch parliament, the Minister of Health allowed staff to offer the pill, up to nine weeks of pregnancy and in the presence of a gynaecologist.

The weak point is that the ship has to pass through a country's waters and dock in its port to meet anyone. On the first voyage, to Ireland in 2001, the group had no proper Dutch licence for abortions, so it gave education only. In 2003 in Poland, protesters threw fake blood and eggs, and the state charged the group with bringing in abortion drugs, then dropped the charges four months later for lack of evidence. In 2004 Portugal's defence minister barred the ship Borndiep from Portuguese waters, and two warships blocked it from reaching Figueira da Foz. The group went to the European Court of Human Rights, which ruled in February 2009 that Portugal had breached freedom of expression under Article 10. Portugal could enforce its abortion law, the court said, but lighter steps such as seizing the pills would have been enough.

That ruling binds only countries in the European human rights system. In October 2012 Morocco's health ministry closed the port of Smir to the ship. In February 2017 at Puerto Quetzal in Guatemala, army troops blocked the pier within a day of docking, a press conference was shut down, and a military ship put the vessel out into international waters. Officials said the crew had told immigration they were tourists. A University of Chicago law journal article sets out the legal argument that would follow. A ship has a right of innocent passage through a territorial sea, meaning it may sail through as long as it does not harm the coastal state's peace or security. Coastal states may stop passage that is not innocent, and may arrest ships breaking local law in those waters. Whether a ship that docks, boards citizens and carries them out for an act banned at home is passing innocently has not been settled.

In April 2017 the ship Adelaide reached Ixtapa in Mexico and ferried women from the Pacific coast out to international waters, and that is the group's most recent reported ship campaign. In 2016 it also used drones and speed boats to deliver pills to Northern Ireland. The case shows that a flag can carry one country's law a short distance beyond another's waters. The law on board is clear, and the open question is whether a coastal state must let the ship reach its people.

china-balloon-2023.mechanism: Countries treat the lower stratosphere as their own airspace, and the United States used force to defend that claim at about 20 kilometres up.
china-balloon-2023.story:
On 4 February 2023 US F-22 fighter jets shot down a Chinese high-altitude balloon over the Atlantic Ocean, just off the coast of South Carolina. Nobody was on board and no casualties were reported. An F-22 fired a short-range Sidewinder missile at it, and debris was recovered from the sea. According to US military officials the balloon was then between 60,000 and 65,000 feet up, about 20 kilometres, above US territorial waters. China called the shooting an unlawful use of force against a civil aircraft. The United States said the balloon was a military surveillance craft violating its sovereignty, and the two governments never agreed on which it was.

The incident is useful because it shows how the law treats a craft at that height. Many people imagine that anything very high up has left the reach of the country below. An analysis by Garry Gumelar Pratama on the Leiden Law School blog in the Netherlands works through the rules step by step. The 1944 Chicago Convention is the main treaty on international flying. Article 1 gives each country complete and exclusive control of the air above its land and territorial waters. A balloon counts as an aircraft under that treaty, even though it flies differently from an aeroplane. At 20 kilometres it was in airspace and not in outer space, so flying there without permission breached US sovereignty.

Whether the US was then allowed to shoot depends on what kind of aircraft it was. The Chicago Convention deals with civil aircraft. An added article, Article 3 bis, tells states not to use weapons against civil aircraft in flight. The United States has not joined that amendment. The analysis says the same rule binds it anyway as customary law, meaning long-standing practice that states treat as law. If the balloon was a state aircraft, as Washington said, the treaty does not cover it. The general rules on countermeasures then apply. A countermeasure is a step a state takes in response to another state's breach, and it has to be proportionate. A claim of necessity also requires that the action was the only way to protect an essential interest from grave and imminent danger.

No treaty sets where airspace ends. A Jakarta Post article on the incident noted that the International Telecommunication Union, the UN body for radio matters, treats stations at 20 to 50 kilometres as high-altitude platforms. Google's parent company flew its Loon internet balloons at around this same height, and it asked each country below for consent.

For anyone hoping to float a home above national control, the case gives a real example. A state defended its claim with a missile at about 20 kilometres, and the legal argument that followed was about which rule permitted the shot and whether it was justified. Neither side argued that the air up there was free.

cloud-nine.mechanism: A home floating in the atmosphere is still in the airspace of the country beneath it, so leaving the ground does not take it outside that country's control.

add_sources.t: IFLScience, Cloud Nine: the 1960s idea to house billions of people in the sky

cloud-nine.story:
Cloud Nine was a design for cities floating in the sky, drawn up around 1960 by the American architect Buckminster Fuller and his architecture partner Shoji Sadao. Their photocollage, Project for Floating Cloud Structures, showed self-contained communities of several thousand people living inside enclosed spheres a mile wide, drifting above the ground. There are two versions of the image, one with smooth silvery spheres and one with the lines of the structure drawn on. A later writer described the idea as housing a future population in the sky. It remained an image and a calculation.

The reasoning came from Fuller's geodesic structures. A geodesic sphere is a thin frame made up of triangles, which spreads stress through the whole shell, and it becomes proportionately stronger as it gets bigger. A sphere's surface grows with the square of its size, while the volume of air inside grows with the cube. So at a mile across, Fuller argued, the frame weighs little compared with the air it holds. A hot air balloon rises because warm air is less dense than the air around it. Fuller said that warming the air inside by a single degree, and letting some of it escape, would lift the whole sphere. A sheet of polyethylene would cover the frame. The sphere could be tethered, left to float, or steered to follow the weather or to serve as emergency shelter.

Critics have doubted that it would work once people live in it. Some who have tried the calculations suggest that floors and living areas would soon make the structure too heavy. How several thousand people would be fed or supplied, or what would happen if the shell were damaged, was never worked out in any detail.

Nothing was built and no government was consulted, so no regulator ever ruled on it. The law it would have met is the 1944 Chicago Convention, the treaty under which each country has full control of the air above its land and territorial waters. A 2023 analysis from Leiden Law School treats even a high-altitude balloon as an aircraft under that treaty. On that reasoning a drifting city would be an aircraft needing permission from each country below it. It would drift across borders with the wind, so it would meet a new permission question at each one. The design is included because it is the clearest statement of the idea that leaving the ground means leaving the state, and the treaty says otherwise.

jp-aerospace-dark-sky-station.mechanism: A platform 43 kilometres up would be below every proposed boundary of outer space, so it would sit in the airspace of whichever country lay beneath it.
jp-aerospace-dark-sky-station.story:
JP Aerospace is a volunteer American group, based in California, that wants to reach orbit by airship instead of by rocket, with a permanently inhabited floating base high over the Earth on the way. Its founder, the engineer John Powell, has worked on high-altitude balloons and rockets since 1979, and he calls the effort the other space program. His aim is to make reaching orbit far cheaper than rocket launches.

The plan, called Airship to Orbit, has three parts, because no single craft could do the whole trip. Sturdy airships would carry people and cargo from the ground up to a floating base called a Dark Sky Station. From that base, huge thin craft filled with helium would climb to orbit, slowly speeding up with electric ion engines. Powell's point is that each type would fail in the other's conditions. The thin orbital craft would be torn apart by winds in the lower atmosphere, and the sturdy ground craft could never reach orbital speed. The technology news site The Register described the stations as mile-wide platforms at 140,000 feet carrying people, while Powell told MSNBC in 2004 that the full-size station in his plan was two miles across. The Register called the concepts for the lower stages feasible and noted that the group had done little flight testing on the orbital craft.

The hardware so far is small. The US Air Force paid for a 175-foot V-shaped airship called Ascender at a cost of about $500,000, according to an officer in 2004. The military wanted it for surveillance and battlefield communications at altitudes above the reach of nearly any attack, and the planned test was to reach 100,000 feet, move between two points and come down safely. On 22 October 2011 an uncrewed craft called Tandem manoeuvred under power at 95,085 feet above the Black Rock Desert in Nevada, and the group claimed that as an airship altitude record. A small prototype station has also flown, using helium balloons linked by carbon-fibre frames. Nobody has lived on any of it, and the group makes no claim to sovereignty.

The law matters if such a base is ever built. At 140,000 feet, about 43 kilometres, it would sit well below both the 100-kilometre and the 80-kilometre lines proposed as the edge of space, so it would be in airspace, where the country below has control under the 1944 Chicago Convention. A station that stayed in one place would be inside one country's air, with that country's permission needed. A station that drifted would need permission from each. Calling it near space does not change that. Whether it would have to be registered as an aircraft, and whose laws would govern people living on board, has never been tested.

karman-line-debate.mechanism: No treaty fixes the boundary between national airspace and outer space, so the band between the highest aircraft and the lowest satellites has no settled legal rules and is open to competing claims.
karman-line-debate.story:
International law has no agreed height at which a country's airspace ends and outer space begins. This gap matters because the two zones have opposite rules. Under the 1944 Chicago Convention, the air above a country's land and territorial waters belongs to that country, so an aircraft needs permission to enter it. Under the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, outer space belongs to no country and any state may use it. A satellite can pass over any country without asking. Neither treaty says where one zone stops and the other begins.

The figure most often used is the Karman line at 100 kilometres (62 miles). It is named after the engineer Theodore von Karman, who worked out in 1956 how high an aeroplane could keep flying. The air thins gradually, and the higher a plane goes the faster it must fly to get enough lift from its wings. At some height it would need to go so fast that it is really orbiting, held up by its speed and not by lift. Von Karman's own calculation put a limit at about 84 kilometres, so the line bearing his name is a rounded figure established later, in the 1960s. The FAI, the international body that keeps air-sport records, uses 100 kilometres to separate aeronautics from astronautics, and many international bodies accept it or something near it. The atmosphere has no sharp edge, and experts disagree about whether any height has physical significance.

Others draw the line elsewhere. The US armed forces call anyone who has flown above 50 miles, about 80 kilometres, an astronaut, and NASA changed from the 100-kilometre figure to match them in 2005. In 2018 the astronomer Jonathan McDowell published a paper in the journal Acta Astronautica proposing 80 kilometres as better suited to the physics and to the orbits actually flown. Another proposal sets the boundary at the lowest point a satellite can reach in orbit, with no fixed number.

Legal writers describe two camps. The spatial camp wants a fixed height, as with a border on the ground. The functional camp would classify an object by what it does, so that a craft on its way to orbit is treated as a spacecraft wherever it is. In 1963 the space lawyer Andrew Haley compared the Karman line to legal measures such as mean sea level, an average that the law agrees to use.

The practical effect is limited for anything low down. Aircraft and balloons fly at about 20 to 40 kilometres, far below every proposed line, so they are in national airspace under any view. Satellites orbit well above every proposed line. The unsettled zone is the band in between, roughly 80 to 100 kilometres in the narrowest view, and nobody can keep a floating or orbiting home there, since the air is too thin to float in and too thick to orbit through for long. A person founding a territory cannot use the missing line as a loophole, because the place they could actually occupy is on one side of it or the other. The matter remains unsettled because no state has needed to resolve it by treaty.

loon-stratosphere.mechanism: Loon treated the stratosphere as national airspace by getting approval from each country its balloons might drift over, even at 20 kilometres up.
loon-stratosphere.story:
Loon was a project to bring internet access to remote areas using balloons that carried mobile network equipment about 20 kilometres up, in the layer of the atmosphere called the stratosphere. It began in 2011 at X, the experimental lab of Google, and in July 2018 became a separate company under Google's parent, Alphabet. It is included here because it is the best real test of flying at that height for years at a time, and it shows that the company behind it asked permission country by country.

Each balloon was made of thin polyethylene plastic, was filled with helium, and stood about 15 metres across. It had no engine. Winds at different heights blow in different directions, so a balloon was steered by rising or sinking until it met a wind going the right way, using US government wind data. People connected through a special antenna on their building, or later through ordinary phones, with signals passed from balloon to balloon and then to a station on the ground. The balloons flew at 18 to 25 kilometres, where the air is calm. One stayed up for a record 312 days, launched from Puerto Rico in May 2019 and landing in Baja, Mexico, in March 2020. When a balloon came down in New Zealand in June 2014, officials briefly sent out emergency services.

Permission was part of the work from the start. The first test in June 2013 launched about 30 balloons in New Zealand in coordination with its Civil Aviation Authority. In July 2015 Google signed an agreement with a government agency in Sri Lanka. After Hurricane Maria in 2017 it applied to the US Federal Communications Commission for authorisation to provide emergency coverage in Puerto Rico, and it was cleared the same day. The balloons also needed radio frequencies, so the company worked with local telephone operators who held licences.

Kenya shows the process most fully. Loon signed a contract with the operator Telkom Kenya in July 2018, then waited until March 2020 for the Kenyan government's formal approval to fly in the stratosphere above the country. The balloons were launched from the United States and navigated to Africa on the wind, which took weeks. Because balloons drift, Loon also signed an airspace agreement with neighbouring Uganda, and a company spokesperson told Reuters that the balloons might pass above Uganda while serving Kenya.

In January 2021 Alphabet announced it was closing Loon. Astro Teller, who ran X, said the road to commercial viability had proven longer and riskier than hoped, and an account on the site Hackaday points to customers in poor areas who could not bring in enough income. Parts of its technology went on in another project in Africa. No country ever had to challenge Loon, because even at 20 kilometres, with no people on board and a large US company behind it, it asked each country along its path for consent. Whether a group wanting to live at that height could get the same consent has never been tested.

bantustans-transkei-bophuthatswana.mechanism: Recognition means other states accepting a place as a state. South Africa granted these homelands independence to serve its own policy, and because no other state accepted them, they never counted as countries in international law.
bantustans-transkei-bophuthatswana.story:
Bantustans, also called homelands, were territories that South Africa's white-minority government set aside for black people under apartheid, its system of legal racial separation. There were ten in South Africa, and four of them were declared independent countries. Most attempts to found a territory start with outsiders pushing against a state. Here a powerful state created the new countries itself, and anti-apartheid movements and every other government rejected them.

The background goes back to 1913, when governments began setting aside reserves for the black population. After the National Party came to power in 1948, Hendrik Verwoerd, first as minister for native affairs and then as prime minister, turned this into a plan. He argued that the reserves were the original homes of South Africa's black peoples. They came to about 13% of the country's land, and the rest was kept for the white minority. The Bantu Self-Government Act of 1959 set out a path for each homeland to become self-governing and then nominally independent. Supporters coined the word Bantustan as a comparison with the partition of India and Pakistan, and it soon became an insult.

The purpose was citizenship. The Bantu Homelands Citizenship Act of 1970 declared black South Africans to be citizens of these homelands, whether or not they had ever lived there, which took away their South African citizenship and the few rights it still gave them. If every black person belonged to a foreign state, South Africa would have no duty to give them a vote. In 1978 the minister Connie Mulder told parliament that, if the policy was carried through, there would be not one black man with South African citizenship. An estimated 3.5 million people were forced from their homes from the 1960s to the 1980s, many of them moved into the Bantustans.

South Africa declared four homelands independent, Transkei in 1976, Bophuthatswana in 1977, Venda in 1979 and Ciskei in 1981. Transkei served as the testing ground for the policy. Each had a government and a constitution set up under South African law. Laws differed from those in South Africa, and wealthy South Africans made use of that, for example by building large casinos such as Sun City in Bophuthatswana, where gambling could be offered.

Recognition is when other states accept a place as a state, and it is what these places could not get. Anti-apartheid movements and every foreign government refused, so only South Africa treated them as countries. They had the outward parts of a state, including territory, people and officials, and that was not enough, because other governments saw them as a device for carrying out apartheid.

In 1985 President P. W. Botha said black people in South Africa proper would no longer lose their citizenship in this way, and that citizens of the independent homelands could reapply for it. The Interim Constitution that came with the end of apartheid in 1994 effectively abolished the Bantustans, and they were absorbed back into South Africa. Bophuthatswana's former leader Lucas Mangope later led a party that contested that ending. For anyone founding a territory, the case shows that a declaration of independence, even with the full support of the neighbouring power, does not make a state in the eyes of others.

denard-comoros.mechanism: A small armed force can take over the government of a weak state, but Denard kept control only while France, the strongest outside power in the region, allowed it.
denard-comoros.story:
Bob Denard was a French mercenary, a soldier for hire, who took part in four attempts to change the government of the Comoros between 1975 and 1995. The Comoros is a small group of islands in the Indian Ocean, between Mozambique and Madagascar, and a former French colony. It has seen more than twenty coups in recent decades. For long periods Denard was its real military power, which makes him one of the few private soldiers who came close to owning a country.

Denard had fought in the Congo and elsewhere in Africa, and for most of his career he had the quiet backing of France and its secret service, which wanted to keep its influence in its former colonies. On 6 July 1975 President Ahmed Abdallah declared the islands independent on his own initiative. Denard then removed him, on the orders of Jacques Foccart, President de Gaulle's adviser on Africa, and Ali Soilih replaced him.

Soilih turned towards socialist politics. On 13 May 1978 Denard returned with 43 men, backed by the government of Rhodesia, and overthrew him, and Soilih was killed on 29 May. The official account that he was shot while trying to escape is not generally believed. Abdallah came back as president.

For the next 11 years Denard held the arrangement together from inside. He commanded the 500-strong presidential guard, became a citizen and acquired hotels and land. The islands also suited outside interests. Denard used them as a base for operations in Mozambique and Angola, and France used them as a way around the embargo on apartheid South Africa. He held the force, while the recognised government remained Abdallah's, so other countries dealt with the president.

In 1989, fearing a coup, Abdallah signed an order for Denard's guard to disarm the regular army. Shortly afterwards he was shot in his office, allegedly by a military officer, and Denard was injured in the same incident. French prosecutors later alleged that Abdallah was killed on Denard's orders because he was about to dismiss him. A few days later Denard agreed to leave after talks with French representatives.

On 27 September 1995 he landed again with 30 to 33 men against President Djohar. This time France was against him. The French army intervened and ended the attempt on 4 October, and he surrendered. A French court gave him a five-year suspended sentence in June 2006. On appeal in July 2007 this became four years with three suspended, which he never served because of poor health. Witnesses at the trial said French intelligence had supported him. He died in October 2007.

The case shows the limit of a very small armed force. Forty-three men could take a weak state. Keeping it depended on a large outside power allowing it, and when France opposed him in 1995 the landing lasted about a week.

free-state-project.mechanism: People who move to a state can vote and win seats there, but that gives them no legal way to take the state out of the United States.
free-state-project.story:
The Free State Project is an American movement that asks people who favour very limited government, known as libertarians, to move to New Hampshire so that they can change its politics. It is the legal, slow version of taking over a territory. It uses house moves and votes, and it works entirely inside the United States.

It began in 2001 when Jason Sorens, then a Ph.D. student at Yale, published an article in The Libertarian Enterprise, in an issue titled "Let's Secede!". He noted that libertarians had failed to elect anyone to federal office, and he proposed forming an independent libertarian nation or, failing that, winning concessions from the US government. He calculated that 20,000 libertarians moving to one small state could change it. After a mixed response he soon backed away from secession, saying it was not part of the project's approach, although it still matters to many members. He has placed the project in an American tradition of political migration that includes Mormon settlers in Utah.

The method was organised and methodical. The group looked for states with fewer than 1.5 million people, where the two main parties spent little on elections. Members voted for New Hampshire in 2003. They signed a pledge to move within five years of the sign-up count reaching 20,000, which it did on 3 February 2016. Those who moved kept ordinary lives, with US citizenship and New Hampshire taxes, and the group holds annual events such as the Liberty Forum and a summer festival at a campground, PorcFest. As an educational non-profit it cannot back candidates.

By May 2022 about 6,232 people had moved. New Hampshire's state House of Representatives has 400 members, so each seat takes few votes. Joel Winters became the first known Free Stater elected, in 2006, as a Democrat. Twelve were elected in 2010, all as Republicans, and 17 held seats in the 2017 to 2018 term. A separate group, the New Hampshire Liberty Alliance, scores lawmakers on libertarian principles, and for the year ending in 2026 it gave 134 of 217 Republican representatives a rating of A- or higher. That figure measures how lawmakers vote and does not count Free Staters.

In 2026 the former executive director Carla Gericke formed a movement called NH Exit Now, which calls for secession. Its website claims that 42% of voters favoured a ballot question in 2022, a figure that comes from the group itself. New Hampshire remains a US state, and no state law can take it out of the Union on its own. The project shows what a modest number of movers can achieve in a small legislature, which is influence over taxes and local rules, and what they cannot achieve by voting, which is leaving the country.

grafton-free-town-project.mechanism: Newcomers can change a small town's budget through ordinary votes, but state and federal law continue to apply to everything there.
grafton-free-town-project.story:
The Free Town Project was an attempt by libertarians, who favour very limited government, to take over the politics of Grafton, a small town in New Hampshire. It was started in 2004 by a splinter group from the Free State Project, the larger movement that had just picked New Hampshire as the state to move to. The idea was to apply the same method at a much smaller scale, because a town can be changed by far fewer voters than a state.

Grafton attracted them because it had no zoning laws, which control how land may be used, and a very low property tax. It was also home to John Babiarz, a Libertarian Party figure who had twice run for governor. No records were kept of how many came, but the population rose from 1,138 in 2000 to 1,340 in 2010, with nearly all the newcomers men. Participants lived in yurts, recreational vehicles, trailers, tents and shipping containers.

New Hampshire towns are governed partly by direct votes of residents, so newcomers could put their ideas on the ballot. They voted through changes that included a 30% cut in the already small town budget and removing funding for the county's senior citizens' council. Lawsuits they filed to set legal precedents raised the town's costs.

Three bear attacks took place in the county after they arrived. A book by Matt Hongoltz-Hetling linked the libertarian presence to rising bear activity, while the state's bear biologist, Andrew Timmins, said in 2023 that nothing suggested the bear population had spiked. Grafton remains an ordinary New Hampshire town under state and federal law, and the project is no longer active as an organised effort.

marinaleda.mechanism: A town can reorganise land and housing through elected office and pressure on the national government without leaving the country or its law.
marinaleda.story:
Marinaleda is a farming town of about 2,562 people in the province of Seville, in Andalusia in southern Spain, known for running its land and housing along collective lines. It is included as a case of people taking control of a place by legal votes and by pressure, while staying fully inside a country. Its people had long been landless day labourers working on large estates. Records from 1751 show 60 houses of labourers who earned two reals for a full day's work.

After the dictator Francisco Franco died in 1975, Spain became a democracy. A farm workers' union was founded in Marinaleda in 1977, and it began occupying large estates the next year. A local group, the Workers' Unity Collective, won 9 of the 11 council seats in the first local elections, in 1979, and its leader Juan Manuel Sánchez Gordillo stayed mayor until he retired in 2023 because of ill health.

What the town wanted was land and better pay, under the slogan "Land to those who work on it". In 1980, 700 people held a 13-day hunger strike over pay and the old hiring system. In 1984 residents occupied the Cordobilla marsh for 30 days to demand irrigation for El Humoso, a farm owned by the Duke of Infantado. In 1985 occupations multiplied and some lasted over 90 days, which led to many legal cases. In 1991, 1,200 hectares of El Humoso were handed over for local use, and between 1992 and 1994 residents occupied government buildings to press further demands.

Daily life grew out of those wins. Irrigation reached the whole farm in 1997, and a cooperative was founded that year to farm it collectively. It grows labour-intensive crops such as artichokes, hot peppers and broad beans, along with olives. A food processing plant followed three years later. People who build their own houses pay no more than 15 euros a month. The town has no municipal police, and during the euro crisis, when 30% of workers in Andalusia were out of work, Marinaleda reported full employment.

It is still an ordinary Spanish municipality, and Spanish law, taxes and courts apply there. Critics say almost 66% of the town's income comes from higher levels of government, while the same source says it received about 6.61% less than the regional average in 2011. Sergio Gómez Reyes succeeded Gordillo as mayor. The case shows how much can be changed through a town hall, including land use and rents, without any claim to separate status.

operation-red-dog-dominica.mechanism: Plotters who need boats and guns must get them somewhere, and that puts them under another country's law. One boat captain's report to US agents stopped this plot before it left New Orleans.
operation-red-dog-dominica.story:
Operation Red Dog was a failed 1981 plot by white supremacists to overthrow the government of Dominica, a small Caribbean island country led by Prime Minister Eugenia Charles, and put former prime minister Patrick John back in power. Those involved included the long-time Ku Klux Klan member Mike Perdue, the German-Canadian Nazi Wolfgang Droege, the Canadian James McQuirter, the American white nationalist Don Black and the plot leader Sydney Burnett-Alleyne.

The aim was to get a country to do business from. In 1979 Perdue outlined a plan to Droege to seize Grenada and set up lucrative businesses there, then changed the target to Dominica, where John and an armed group of his supporters were to meet them. Burnett-Alleyne later told a Barbados newspaper that he had wanted to add Dominica's land to Barbados and carry out a large industrial project. Perdue testified that he got $10,000 from a Memphis lawyer and used $70,000 collected from businessmen for weapons, dynamite and scouting trips.

The plan was to charter a boat in New Orleans, sail to Dominica and go ashore in rubber boats. That meant finding a captain. In February 1981 the original captain and crew backed out, so Perdue approached another captain, Michael Howell, a Vietnam War veteran, telling him the CIA needed his boat. Howell went to the US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms (ATF), the federal agency that enforces gun laws.

John was arrested in Dominica on 25 April. On 27 April, Droege and eight other men were arrested at a marina in New Orleans as they prepared to board, with automatic weapons, shotguns, dynamite and a Nazi flag. Three undercover agents were in the group, and nobody was hurt.

A plot of this kind has to begin in some country, and buying guns and hiring a boat there falls under that country's law, whatever the target. A 2008 book by the Canadian journalist Stewart Bell, Bayou of Pigs, tells the story.

rajneeshpuram-antelope.mechanism: Moving enough voters into a small area can legally win control of its local government, but state and federal criminal law continue to apply to those who hold it.
rajneeshpuram-antelope.story:
Rajneeshpuram was a city built by followers of the Indian spiritual teacher Bhagwan Shree Rajneesh on a huge ranch in Wasco County, central Oregon, in the 1980s. It is the fullest American example of a group using ordinary local law to create its own government. After a bombing over land use at his ashram in Pune, India, Rajneesh sent his secretary, Ma Anand Sheela, to find a new site in the United States, which appeared to promise religious freedom.

In 1981 they bought the 64,281-acre Big Muddy Ranch, about 100 square miles, for $5.75 million. Within three years they had turned it into a city of up to 7,000 people with a fire department, police, restaurants, malls, townhouses, an airstrip and a post office. The followers, called sannyasins, lived and worked there as a commune, and Sheela acted as its leader in practice. The police, called the Peace Force, carried semi-automatic weapons, which alarmed their neighbours.

Oregon's land-use rules limited what could be built on farmland, and the group 1000 Friends of Oregon challenged the project on those grounds. A city would have more freedom. Antelope, the nearest town, had under 60 people. The followers bought lots there, and Antelope denied them a business permit for a mail-order office. As more moved in, residents voted in April 1982 on dissolving their own town to avoid a takeover, and the followers had enough votes to defeat the plan. In May 1982 the ranch voted to become a city in its own right.

Legal challenges followed. Oregon's attorney general argued that the city merged church and state, because a religious group owned all its land and ran its government. That raises a question under the US Constitution, which bars government from establishing a religion. Meanwhile the leaders tried to win control of the county. In 1984 some of them, led by Sheela, poisoned the salad bars of ten restaurants with salmonella bacteria to lower turnout in county elections, sickening 751 people and sending 45 to hospital. In September 1984 they also bused in upwards of 4,000 homeless people, one aim being to add voters. A plot to kill Charles Turner, the US attorney for Oregon, followed in 1985.

The criminal law then ended what the zoning cases had not. Rajneesh was accused of immigration violations and entered a plea in which he did not admit guilt, agreeing to leave the country, and the commune broke up in 1985. A federal judge ruled against the city that year, too late to matter, and Oregon courts later upheld it. The ranch was sold in 1988 at a sheriff's auction for $4.5 million and is now a camp run by the Christian group Young Life.

The case shows that moving in voters can legally win a local government, and that the result stays subject to state courts, federal prosecutors and immigration officers. The commune's end came through prosecutions for crimes its leaders committed while trying to protect that position.

seychelles-1981-coup.why: Wikipedia counts 54 mercenaries including Hoare, while the entry's figures (9 plus 44) give 53. The entry's figures are kept.
seychelles-1981-coup.mechanism: A plot against a recognised government depends on its secrecy, and this one was exposed by one bag search at the airport. South Africa, which encouraged it, later faced international condemnation.
seychelles-1981-coup.story:
In November 1981 a group of mercenaries, soldiers for hire, led by Mike Hoare tried to overthrow the government of Seychelles, an island country in the Indian Ocean, with encouragement from apartheid South Africa. Seychelles became independent in 1976 with James Mancham as president and France-Albert René as prime minister. In 1977 René's supporters seized power while Mancham was in London, and René became president. Mancham then sought South African help to return, and he was directed to Hoare, a veteran of mercenary wars in the Congo.

South African officials ran the plan under the code name Operation Angela, with its army's intelligence division in charge after a dispute with the National Intelligence Service. Of the force, 27 were members of the South African Defence Force, with ex-Rhodesian soldiers, former Congo mercenaries and an intelligence agent making up most of the rest. Hoare advised raising $5 million, but only $300,000 was found.

The plan was simple. Nine men went ahead to Mahé, the main island, to find targets and rally dissident soldiers. On 25 November 1981, 44 more, including Hoare, flew in on a chartered plane, disguised as rugby players and members of a beer-drinking charity club, with weapons hidden in their luggage. They were to scatter to hotels, wait for several days until René held a cabinet meeting, and then seize parliament and other key places.

It failed at the airport. All but two had passed customs when a security supervisor made a thorough search of one man's bag and found an AK-47. A long gunfight followed, and one soldier and one mercenary died. An Air India airliner had landed during the fighting. Most of the mercenaries boarded it and made the captain fly them to Durban in South Africa.

South Africa then had a problem of its own making. It did not charge them with attempting a coup, only with aviation offences. Most were freed at first and charged later, and 34 of them served about four months. Hoare's sentence was ten years in Wikipedia's account and 20 in the Irish Times obituary, and he was released in May 1985 under an amnesty after about three years.

Those left behind fared worse. A Seychelles court sentenced four captured men to death for treason on 6 July 1982 and two others to prison. All six were pardoned after talks and a $3 million payment to René. A UN inquiry and South Africa's later Truth and Reconciliation Commission condemned South Africa's role, although a South African judge cleared the government at the time. The case shows how little it takes to end such a plan, since it depends on secrecy, and one customs check was enough. It also shows that a state behind a plot will still act to protect itself when it fails, leaving the men captured on the islands to be bargained over.

slab-city.mechanism: When a government does not enforce its rules, people can live freely on public land, but this lasts only as long as the owner leaves them alone.
slab-city.story:
Slab City is an off-the-grid camp in the desert of Imperial County, southern California, whose residents call it "the last free place". It lies on about 640 acres near the east shore of the Salton Sea, four miles from the small town of Niland, and has no local government. It is an example of how people can live with little state presence inside a rich country, without any claim to independence.

Its name comes from the concrete slabs left behind when the US Marines dismantled Camp Dunlap, a 631-acre artillery training base opened in 1942. All the buildings were gone by 1956. In 1961 the Department of Defense passed the land to California by a quitclaim deed, a transfer with no promises about the title. A few veterans who had worked at the base stayed, followed by drifters and then by owners of recreational vehicles looking for free camping outside Palm Springs.

The Washington Post reported in 2020 that the population might reach 4,000 in winter, when retirees arrive to escape the cold, and fall to about 150 in summer. People live in vehicles and self-built shelters, and they pay no rent. There are no public services. Many use generators or solar panels for electricity. Clean water is dispensed from a tank at the community church, and people go to Niland for shopping and find proper law enforcement there. Residents, who call themselves Slabbies, have set up a free lending library and an outdoor music venue called The Range. Nearby is Salvation Mountain, a painted adobe hill that the settler Leonard Knight spent almost 30 years building, which became widely known after the 2007 film Into the Wild.

The freedom rests on a government's decision to do nothing. Reports conflict on who owns the land. Some say the state of California, and others from 1993 say a building contractor. In 2015 residents formed a community group to try to prevent a sale. As of 2021 California had not decided to sell, and its State Lands Commission was considering an appraisal and a clean-up of military waste. California and US law still apply to the camp, though they are largely not enforced there. Residents have no title to what they build, so a sale or a clean-up order could end the arrangement. The camp has lasted for decades on remote land with little enforcement, and no document protects it.

wonga-coup-equatorial-guinea.mechanism: A privately funded armed takeover has to pass through other countries on its way, and this one was stopped at an airport in Zimbabwe. One backer was then convicted under South Africa's law against mercenary activity.
wonga-coup-equatorial-guinea.story:
The Wonga Coup was a failed 2004 plot by foreign mercenaries, soldiers for hire, to overthrow Teodoro Obiang, president of the oil-rich African country of Equatorial Guinea, and replace him with the exiled politician Severo Moto, who lived in Spain. It was organised by mainly British financiers. Prosecutors said Moto offered the group $1.8 million and oil rights. It shows what a modern private attempt to take a state looks like, with investors, a chartered plane and bank transfers.

The man in charge on the ground was Simon Mann, a former British special forces officer who had gone on to private military work with companies including Sandline International. He later called himself the manager and not the architect. He ran payments through a Guernsey firm, Logo Logistics. The Lebanese oil billionaire Ely Calil was alleged to have raised money, and he denied knowing about the plot. Bank details showed a payment of $134,000 from a JH Archer, and the British politician Jeffrey Archer denied prior knowledge.

A coup needs guns and they have to be bought somewhere. Equatorial Guinea is on the west coast of Africa. On 7 March 2004 a Boeing 727 from South Africa landed at Harare airport in Zimbabwe, where weapons worth about £100,000 were to be loaded. Zimbabwean police impounded it, with three crew and 64 former soldiers on board, and arrested Mann by the runway. Mann said the weapons were for guarding diamond mines in Congo. On 9 March Nick du Toit, a South African who helped with recruitment, weapons and logistics, and 14 others were arrested in Equatorial Guinea, and du Toit testified that Mann had recruited him to install Moto.

The name comes from a letter Mann wrote from prison asking for "a large splodge of wonga", British slang for money. The letter also used nicknames thought to refer to backers, including Scratcher, thought to be Mark Thatcher. On 13 January 2005 Mark Thatcher, son of the former British prime minister Margaret Thatcher, pleaded guilty in South Africa to attempting to breach its anti-mercenary law by agreeing to charter a helicopter he suspected might be used for mercenary activity. Al Jazeera reported he had paid $275,000 for the charter. He was fined 3 million rand, about $500,000, and given a four-year prison term suspended for five years.

Equatorial Guinea also sued alleged financiers in London, using ordinary civil courts. Mann served three years in Zimbabwe and was then extradited to Equatorial Guinea, where he was sentenced in 2008 to more than 34 years. President Obiang pardoned him on 2 November 2009 on humanitarian grounds, and he returned to England, where he died in May 2025. The case shows that a private takeover has to pass through other countries' airports, banks and laws on its way. Several of them, including South Africa with its anti-mercenary law, can punish it long before anyone lands.

bir-tawil-kingdom-of-north-sudan.mechanism: This case tests whether a private person can acquire land that no government claims. International law allows only states to take terra nullius (land belonging to no state), so Heaton's flag and website gave him no legal ownership.
bir-tawil-kingdom-of-north-sudan.story:
Bir Tawil is a stretch of 2,060 square kilometres of hot desert on the border between Egypt and Sudan that neither country claims. It is the best-known piece of land on Earth with no state claiming it, and it has no permanent settlement. In 2014 an American farmer declared it a kingdom.

Its status comes from two lines the British drew when they controlled the region. In 1899 an agreement between Britain and Egypt set the border along a straight line, the 22nd parallel of latitude. In 1902 the British drew a separate administrative line meant to follow how local tribes actually used the land. It placed Bir Tawil, grazing land used by the Ababda people based near Aswan, under Egypt, and it placed the Hala'ib Triangle, a larger area on the Red Sea, under Sudan. Egypt now relies on the 1899 line and Sudan on the 1902 line, because each line gives that country Hala'ib. Claiming Bir Tawil would mean giving up the argument for the more valuable land, so both countries say it belongs to the other.

On 16 June 2014, his daughter Emily's seventh birthday, Jeremiah Heaton, a farmer from Virginia, planted a blue flag there and announced the Kingdom of North Sudan on Facebook. He had told her she could become a princess, and he had gone looking for land that would make it possible. He said he asked for permission in Cairo to make the trip. He then planned an agricultural research centre that he compared to Noah's Ark, with more than 1,000 scientists working on water and farming. He estimated the project would take at least $2 billion and launched an online fundraising campaign in May 2015 seeking up to $45 million. He offered titles of nobility for $25, a street name for $1,000 and the right to name the capital city for $1.75 million. He also applied for observer status at the United Nations. A film deal was reported.

The law on empty land gives him little. Terra nullius means land belonging to no state, and international law lets a state, acting as a state, take such land. A private person cannot acquire it by planting a flag, and a person's new state only exists in the eyes of the law if other states treat it as one. Heaton himself reached the land by way of Cairo. Noam Leshem, a geographer at Durham University, told Al Jazeera that the land's status is ambiguous and that tribes still use it. Empty on a map does not mean unused.

No government has recognised the kingdom, meaning none has accepted it as a state, and no one has settled there. No state or court has tested the claim either, since neither Egypt nor Sudan has needed to respond to it.

bir-tawil-later-claimants.mechanism: Private people who claim the same land have no court to settle it between them, because only states can hold title to territory in international law and no state is involved here.
bir-tawil-later-claimants.story:
