After the American farmer Jeremiah Heaton claimed Bir Tawil in 2014, several other people declared their own states on the same land. Bir Tawil is a strip of desert between Egypt and Sudan that neither country claims, because each relies on a border line that gives the strip to the other. Its unclaimed status has drawn such announcements, most of them made online.

In November 2017 Suyash Dixit, a 24-year-old businessman from Indore in India, flew from Cairo to Abu Simbel, drove in on 4 November, planted sunflower seeds and declared the Kingdom of Dixit, asking the United Nations for recognition. A day later the Russian Dmitry Zhikharev announced a Kingdom of Middle Earth, accused Heaton and Dixit of faking their visits, and said he had declared himself ruler in December 2014. In September 2019 a video circulated in which the Michigan businesswoman Nadera Nassif, speaking from Odessa in Ukraine, named herself prime minister of a Kingdom of the Yellow Mountain, and said it would solve the problem of displaced people and refugees. Egypt and Sudan both refused to accept it. The London barrister Dwain Coward told the magazine VICE he had set up a company in Sudan and sent terms to tribal chiefs, because gold miners using mercury were damaging the land.

There are real people on the ground, and none of the claimants rules them. VICE reports that the only people working there are migrants from Sudan who dig for gold and sell it in Khartoum, so the land is reached and used from Sudan. These overlapping claims show a further problem. If two people say they own a house, a court decides. Here no court would hear it, because only states can hold title to territory in international law, and no state is involved. No government or international body has recognised any of these claims.

clipperton-arbitration.mechanism: On a completely uninhabited territory, a state's clear intention, public notice and a brief presence can be enough to gain ownership, and later absence does not lose it unless the state means to abandon the land.
clipperton-arbitration.story:
Clipperton is an uninhabited coral ring around a lagoon in the eastern Pacific Ocean, about 1,080 kilometres southwest of Mexico. The dispute between France and Mexico over who owned it produced one of the main rulings on how a state can claim empty land. Anyone who thinks a remote island is free for the taking needs to understand what this ruling requires.

On 17 November 1858 the French naval lieutenant Victor le Coat de Kerwéguen, on a merchant ship half a mile offshore, proclaimed French sovereignty over the island. A boat landed a few men, nobody left any sign of possession, and notice was sent to the Hawaiian government and printed in a Honolulu newspaper. Then nothing happened for 39 years. American guano miners began working the island in the early 1890s, collecting bird droppings used as fertiliser. In 1897 France found three people there working for an American company. A Mexican gunboat arrived that December and replaced the American flag with Mexico's. Mexico claimed the island as an inheritance from Spain, based on old Spanish records.

On 2 March 1909 the two countries agreed to arbitration, meaning they would let a chosen judge decide and would accept the result, and they picked King Victor Emmanuel III of Italy. His award came on 28 January 1931. He first asked whether Spain, and so Mexico, had really held the island before 1858, and found that Mexico had not proved it. So in 1858 the island was territorium nullius, land belonging to no state, and open to whoever properly took it.

The main question was what taking requires. Normally, he said, physical possession is needed, meaning a state must really be present. On a completely uninhabited island, however, a state's arrival can complete possession at once, because no one is there to control and little is needed to control it. The French notice in Honolulu was public enough. France's 39 years of doing nothing did not lose the island, because it had never meant to give it up. A state keeps a place unless it intends to abandon it.

Clipperton remains French territory and has no permanent residents. It has a real value to France because of the rule giving coastal states rights over nearby seas. The exclusive economic zone, a sea area where a state controls fishing and seabed resources, around the island covers 431,273 square kilometres, and French naval patrols are infrequent, so illegal fishing goes on there.

A private settler can take nothing from this ruling except a warning. The test applies to states. A lieutenant acting for France could claim the island from a boat, while a person arriving today with a flag would find that an old, barely visible French claim is still valid.

couto-misto.mechanism: Long custom can produce working self-rule, but custom gives no protection once the neighbouring states agree by treaty to end it.
couto-misto.story:
Couto Misto was a group of three villages on the border of Spain and Portugal that governed itself for centuries, belonging fully to neither kingdom. The villages, Santiago de Rubiás, Rubiás and Meaus, lie in what is now the province of Ourense in Galicia, and a small uninhabited strip went with them. It covered about 26.7 square kilometres and had about 1,000 people by an estimate from 1859.

A couto was a medieval district marked by boundary stones and exempt from the king's authority, with its own economic and legal arrangements. Through overlapping feudal ties, this one escaped control by both crowns. Its origin is unclear, and one source dates it to the 10th century. Portugal abolished its coutos between 1692 and 1790, after which this one was also free of feudal ties and ran in practice as an independent state. It is an old example of a place that nobody founded. It was left over by history, and it survived because neither neighbour pressed the point.

Daily life had unusual privileges. Residents paid no tax to either country, did not serve in either army, could grant asylum to outsiders and could refuse entry to foreign troops. Decisions came from an assembly of the people, and a judge, called the Juiz, acted as head of state. The capital was Santiago de Rubiás. People spoke Portuguese, Spanish and Galician. One of the last judges, Delfim Modesto Brandão, took office in January 1863 and left memoirs about it.

The end came through diplomacy. The Treaty of Lisbon, dated 29 September 1864, set the border between Spain and Portugal. It divided the territory, with Spain taking the three villages and most of the land and Portugal taking the uninhabited strip. The treaty was made between the two kingdoms. The takeover was completed in 1868.

The case shows that custom can sustain real self-government for a long time, and that it gives no protection once the states around it agree. Two neighbouring powers can settle a border between themselves, and a small place in between has no standing to stop them.

free-republic-of-verdis.mechanism: Croatia physically controls the river bank, and that decides who may stay there, whatever documents a claimant holds. Liberland met the same result on a larger scale.
free-republic-of-verdis.story:
Verdis is a self-declared state on a 128-acre strip of forest and marsh on the Danube river, between Croatia and Serbia, in an area known as Pocket 3. It is roughly the size of Vatican City. It exists as a claim because the two countries disagree about their river border. Serbia says the border follows the middle of the Danube. Croatia says it follows old land records, which were drawn when the river ran along a different course. That dispute dates from 1947 and was never settled when Yugoslavia broke up, and it leaves small pockets of land that Serbia does not claim and that Croatia regards as disputed.

Daniel Jackson, born in Australia to British parents, had the idea at about age 14 and helped declare the state in 2019, after finding the plot through people he met online. He said it was meant as a neutral base for humanitarian groups, and that Liberland, a similar claim nearby, partly inspired it. He told NBC the group planted a flag in 2023 and did survey work.

Most of Verdis has existed online. It had received about 15,000 citizenship applications, at a $16 fee, and had accepted about 350 to 400 people, who were issued passports. Jackson says some have been used at borders, though no government recognises them.

In October 2023 settlers tried to set up a permanent camp on the land. Jackson said Croatian authorities destroyed it within days, arrested the group and told them to leave or be deported. He received a permanent ban from Croatia and the others received three-month bans. He now runs the project from Dover in England and says he plans a legal fight. The difficulty for a person arriving at this land is practical. Croatia physically controls the bank, so it decides who stays, and a claim that nobody wants the land does not bind the country that patrols it.

No government recognises Verdis as a state. Liberland, on a nearby pocket, met the same result on a larger scale.

free-state-of-bottleneck.mechanism: An error in drawing a military map can leave people outside any working government, and in this case they set up their own administration to run things until Germany took the area back.
free-state-of-bottleneck.story:
The Free State of Bottleneck was a tiny area on the Rhine river in western Germany that ran itself from 1919 to 1920 after a quirk in Allied occupation maps cut it off from the rest of the country. It is one of the clearest cases of a territory created by accident.

After the First World War ended in 1918, Allied armies occupied Germany west of the Rhine and marked out three half-circles of 30 kilometres radius on the eastern bank, around Cologne, Koblenz and Mainz. The French and American half-circles did not quite meet. That left a narrow strip holding the Wisper valley, the towns of Lorch and Kaub and several villages. Occupied zones lay on two sides and the Rhine to the south-west, and there was no road or railway to the north-east, so the area was cut off from Germany and its government. Trains were not allowed to stop there. Locals declared a free state on 10 January 1919, named after its bottleneck shape on the map.

About 17,000 people lived there. Lorch was the capital, and its mayor, Edmund Pnischeck, was elected president and ran the administration for its whole life. People had to feed and heat themselves with nobody responsible for supplying them. Pnischeck's first action was to have a temporary road built to unoccupied Germany. Goods and post came in mostly by smuggling, some of it by ship at night. Once a French coal train from Rüdesheim was hijacked and taken into the strip, and the coal was shared out for heating. The territory printed its own emergency money, with a verse saying nowhere was finer than the Free State of Bottleneck, and it issued passports to its citizens. It planned an embassy in Berlin and relations with other countries, but neither happened.

Its self-rule ended on 1 July 1920, after the German army put down the Ruhr uprising, and the area returned to the Prussian province of Hesse-Nassau. A 1923 end date, tied to the French occupation of the Ruhr, also circulates, but Pnischeck called it nonsense. The area is now part of the Rhine Gorge World Heritage Site.

Bottleneck was never a state seeking independence. Its people were Germans cut off by a mapping error, and they set up an administration because no one else could reach them. Its currency and passports were practical tools for a temporary problem. It ended without a contest when the reason for it disappeared.

island-of-palmas.mechanism: A country gains title to territory by actually governing it continuously and peacefully. Discovering it or being close to it does not beat that.
island-of-palmas.story:
Palmas, now called Miangas and part of Indonesia, is an island about 2.6 kilometres long and 1 kilometre wide between the Philippines and Indonesia. It had little economic or strategic value and about 750 people in 1932. A dispute over it produced one of the best-known rulings on how countries gain territory, and that ruling is still the first thing anyone must understand before claiming land.

In 1898 Spain gave the Philippines to the United States by a treaty whose boundaries took in Palmas. In 1906 the United States found that the Netherlands, then the colonial power in what is now Indonesia, also claimed it. On 23 January 1925 the two countries agreed to binding arbitration, meaning they would accept a chosen judge's decision, and the Swiss lawyer Max Huber acted as sole arbitrator under the Permanent Court of Arbitration.

The United States made three arguments. Spain had discovered the island, the island lay close to the Philippines, and the United States had inherited whatever Spain owned. Each argument matches an idea many people still hold, that finding a place or being next to it makes it yours.

Huber decided on 4 April 1928. He wrote that discovering land gives at most an inchoate title, a starting claim that must be completed by actual possession within a reasonable time. A person who finds an empty plot and walks away has not acquired it. He rejected contiguity, the idea that being nearby is enough to give ownership, because nearness gives no clear rule for who owns what. Spain could also pass on only what it really held. What counted was governing. He held that the continuous and peaceful display of the functions of a state is as good as a title, and the Dutch, working through local rulers and their treaties with them, had shown this from 1700 to 1906. Local arrangements on a small, distant island can be enough, since a state need only govern to the degree the place requires. The whole island was therefore Dutch territory, and it later passed to Indonesia.

The rule has two sides for anyone founding a territory. A claim on paper loses to a government that actually runs the place, which encourages actual occupation. But the test is the display of a state's functions by a state, peacefully and with no serious challenge. A private group landing on land already governed by a state cannot meet it, and that state will challenge them at once.

islands-of-refreshment.mechanism: Living on an unclaimed island and declaring it yours creates no title that other states must accept, and Britain took Tristan da Cunha by sending troops, without any dealings with the settler who had claimed it.
islands-of-refreshment.story:
The Islands of Refreshment was the name Jonathan Lambert, an American sailor from Salem, Massachusetts, gave to the Tristan da Cunha islands in the South Atlantic when he declared them his own. These remote islands then had no permanent residents.

Lambert arrived on the whaler Grand Turk in December 1810, or January 1811 by another account, with two other men, later joined by a fourth. He declared himself Lord and Prince of Tristan da Cunha and its two neighbouring islands, Inaccessible and Nightingale, and the islands his property. He made his living by hunting seals and selling their oil to passing ships.

The scheme lasted little more than a year. Lambert drowned near Inaccessible Island on 27 May 1812, with the sailor Andrew Millet. By the end of that year only one of the four men, Tommaso Corri from Livorno in Italy, was still alive, and he stayed on as a farmer.

On 14 August 1816 Britain annexed the islands by sending a garrison and made them a dependency of its Cape Colony in South Africa. It had two reasons. It wanted to stop the islands being used as a base to free Napoleon from his prison on Saint Helena, and it wanted to deter the United States, whose navy had used them in the War of 1812. Britain did not need to answer Lambert's claim, since he was dead and no state had ever accepted it. The garrison left in 1817, but some of its members stayed and started the community that still lives there. By 1824 there were twenty-two men and three women. Tristan da Cunha remains a British territory, with 243 people in 2021.

The case shows a pattern seen again and again. A private person can really live on an empty island and declare it theirs. A state can then take it for reasons that have nothing to do with that person, and the state's claim is the one other countries recognise.

kingdom-of-enclava.mechanism: Land that looks unclaimed on a map may be under active dispute between states, and in that case the argument that it is terra nullius (land belonging to no state) fails as soon as those states speak.
kingdom-of-enclava.story:
The Kingdom of Enclava was a self-declared state on a small plot on the border of Slovenia and Croatia, near the village of Brezovica pri Metliki in southeastern Slovenia. The border there is tangled, with a small Croatian enclave, a piece of one country surrounded by another, already sitting inside Slovenian land.

In 2015 the Polish tourist Piotr Wawrzynkiewicz read on Wikipedia that a small piece of land there was unclaimed, and he declared it a kingdom. Newspapers around the world reported the story. The Slovenian foreign ministry then said the plot was part of a territorial claim of its own, also claimed by Croatia, which was going before the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague. So an online reference page had called the land unclaimed while two governments were arguing over it in an international forum.

On 29 June 2017 the court ruled that a disputed 2.4-hectare parcel beside the enclave, the same parcel claimed as Enclava, belonged to Slovenia. That created a second Croatian enclave. Croatia refused to implement the decision. Wawrzynkiewicz moved his project to an unclaimed area on the Croatia-Serbia border.

Nothing is known of anyone living on the plot. The case is included because it shows a mistake many claimants make. Terra nullius, land belonging to no state, is a legal status, and a gap on a map or a line in a web article does not establish it. A border that looks unclear usually means two states each say the land is theirs.

kowloon-walled-city.mechanism: When two states each decline to use their authority over a place, residents and criminal groups fill the space, but the states' legal claims remain in force and can be used as soon as they agree to act.
kowloon-walled-city.story:
Kowloon Walled City was an extremely crowded settlement in Hong Kong that for decades was largely outside the control of both Britain and China. It shows what grows up when two governments each leave a place alone. Nobody set out to found it.

The site began as a military outpost and was rebuilt as a Chinese coastal fort in 1847, after Britain took Hong Kong Island. In 1898 Britain leased the neighbouring New Territories from China for 99 years. The lease left out the fort, which had about 700 people, and China was allowed to keep officials there. So it stayed a Chinese enclave, a piece of one country's land inside another's. Britain soon claimed that it owned the site anyway, and each government kept its legal claim for the next 90 years. By 1940 only the old official building, a school and one house remained. In the Second World War Japanese forces demolished the wall and used the stone to expand nearby Kai Tak Airport.

In 1933 Hong Kong announced plans to clear it and rehouse 436 squatters. A further attempt to drive people out failed in 1948, and after that the British left most matters alone. Neither government wanted to enforce its authority there. Refugees from the Chinese Civil War poured in. Developers in the 1960s built new blocks on top of older ones, with no planning rules, until about 300 buildings stood packed together.

From the 1950s to the 1970s triads, Chinese criminal gangs, controlled the place, with gambling, prostitution and drug trafficking, until police raids in the 1970s reduced their power. Most residents had nothing to do with crime. They ran small factories, schools, clinics and dental practices with no regulation, and some formed groups to organise and improve daily life. Sanitary conditions stayed far behind the rest of Hong Kong. By 1987 about 33,000 people lived on 2.6 hectares, some 1.2 million per square kilometre.

The legal limbo ended once the two governments stopped disagreeing. In their 1984 Joint Declaration Britain and China agreed that Hong Kong would return to China, so the question of who held authority no longer mattered, and on 14 January 1987 they announced demolition. Compensating the residents cost HK$2.7 billion. The buildings were pulled down between March 1993 and April 1994.

The Walled City was never independent and never claimed to be. It shows that a gap between two states can last a very long time and hold tens of thousands of people, and that residents have no rights in that gap that survive an agreement between the states. It also shows who fills the gap. Without police and courts, gangs took the role for about two decades, and people relied on their own associations for services.

liberland.mechanism: A difference between two countries' border claims does not make land free to take, because the country that physically controls it can treat anyone entering as an illegal border crosser, whatever documents they hold.
liberland.story:
Liberland is a self-declared country on a strip of flood-prone forest on the Danube river, between Croatia and Serbia. It is the best-known modern attempt to found a state on land said to be unclaimed, and it has become the standard test of whether that argument works.

The background is a border disagreement left by the break-up of Yugoslavia. Serbia places the border on the deepest channel of the river. Croatia uses old land records that follow the river's 19th-century course, which has since moved. That left pockets on the west bank that Serbia does not claim and that Croatia does not treat as settled Croatian land. On 13 April 2015 the Czech politician Vit Jedlicka, a member of the Czech Party of Free Citizens, planted a flag on the largest pocket, 7 square kilometres of floodplain called Gornja Siga, and declared a state where paying tax would be optional. He argued that no nation claimed the land, so he could take it as terra nullius, land belonging to no state. The land has no infrastructure or residents, and a journalist who visited in April 2015 found one abandoned house.

Croatia does not accept the argument. It treats the land as part of an unsettled border dispute, says visitors must obey Croatian law, and has been detaining them since May 2015, and it has frequently blocked access. Jedlicka spent a night in custody and was fined. Serbia calls the project frivolous and says it is no threat so long as it stays on the western bank. So its people work from elsewhere. Jedlicka lives in Prague, supporters gather in Serbian villages and on houseboats, and the group has hired a lobbyist in the United States, registered with the Justice Department, to seek recognition.

The country has mostly existed online. Its planned currency is a cryptocurrency called Merit, with bitcoin and gold also promoted, and a registry and voting system would run on a blockchain, an online shared ledger. Passports are sold to paying supporters, at $10,000 by Wikipedia's account and at $5,000 or equivalent for full citizenship by Wired's. Wired magazine reported that 700,000 people had registered support and about 6,000 were paying e-residents, meaning members who hold an online form of citizenship, and that about 1,000 had paid by 2023.

In August 2023, after Croatia joined the Schengen area of free travel in Europe, supporters built wooden shelters. Police arrested Jedlicka on 9 September and banned him from Croatia for five years. On 21 September a private company, watched by police, took down and removed the camp, and the settlers moved to houseboats and a village on the Serbian side.

Nobody lives on the land, and no recognised state accepts it as a country. The legal point is that two states disagreeing about a border is not the same as no state having a claim. Even if the land had been truly unclaimed, the case law on empty land concerns states taking it, and a private declaration needs others to accept it. Croatia's position is the one that counts on the ground, because it controls the bank.

neutral-moresnet.mechanism: A place can stay outside either neighbour's rule for generations if both agree to leave it that way, but the arrangement ends when one of them changes its position. This one was a condominium, an area governed jointly by two states.
neutral-moresnet.story:
Neutral Moresnet was a tiny triangle of land between what are now Belgium and Germany that for more than a century belonged to neither of its neighbours. It was a condominium, an area governed jointly by two states, and it arose from an argument over one mine.

After Napoleon's defeat, the Congress of Vienna redrew the map of Europe, and the Netherlands and Prussia had to fix their border. Both wanted a valuable zinc mine called Vieille Montagne or Altenberg. On 26 June 1816 they split the Moresnet district in three. The Dutch took one village, Prussia took another, and the mine and its village became a neutral area of 3.5 square kilometres, run by one commissioner from each side. Belgium took over the Dutch role after becoming independent in 1830.

Daily life revolved around the mine. Napoleon's old legal codes stayed in force, and because the territory had no court of its own, judges from Belgium and Prussia came in to hear cases. The mine company dominated, running housing, shops, a hospital and a bank. Taxes were low, there were no import tariffs, and residents counted as stateless, citizens of no country, so they had no passports of their own. From 1883 it used a black, white and blue flag. The population rose from 256 in 1815 to 4,668 in 1914.

People also tried to make something more of it. In 1903 a casino opened and then closed after pressure from Kaiser Wilhelm II. In 1908 the mine doctor Wilhelm Molly proposed making it an Esperanto-speaking state named Amikejo, and a rally for the idea was held on 13 August.

The neighbours' agreement ended with the First World War. Germany invaded Belgium in 1914 and annexed the territory in 1915. The Treaty of Versailles then gave it to Belgium, and from January 1920 it became the Belgian municipality of Kelmis.

Neutral Moresnet was a joint arrangement of its neighbours and never an independent state. Its status was granted and could be withdrawn by the two states that shared it. Residents enjoyed a real gap, with low tax and few obligations, for 104 years. The arrangement ended when one of the neighbours went to war.

no-mans-land-cimarron-territory.mechanism: Land can lie inside a country's borders and still have no local government. People lived there for decades without valid title, because only Congress could set up a government and legal land system for it.
no-mans-land-cimarron-territory.story:
No Man's Land was a strip of the American plains, now the Oklahoma panhandle, that belonged to no state or territory for 40 years. It is 166 miles long and 34 miles wide. This is what a legal blank looks like inside a country. The land was clearly part of the United States, yet no local government or land office covered it.

It came about through the politics of slavery. When Texas joined the United States in 1845, federal law barred slavery north of latitude 36 degrees 30 minutes. Under the Compromise of 1850, Texas gave up its land north of that line. Later laws fixed New Mexico's boundary at the 103rd meridian and, in 1854, Kansas's at the 37th parallel. Each law drew its own line for its own reasons, and nobody assigned the strip left between them. It was officially called the Public Land Strip.

Cattlemen moved in after the Civil War and made their own rules for land and disputes. In 1885 the US Supreme Court ruled that the strip was not part of the neighbouring Cherokee lands. In 1886 Interior Secretary L.Q.C. Lamar declared it public land open to squatters, people who settle without title. That started the real trouble. The Homestead Act gave settlers free land, but it could only work on surveyed land, and this land had never been officially surveyed. So settlers could live on a farm and still never own it.

Thousands came anyway and surveyed their own claims. Without a court or a sheriff, they needed some means of keeping order and recording who held what. They set up a government called Cimarron Territory, with its own law code and Owen G. Chase at its head, and asked Congress to recognise it in February and December 1887.

Congress did not. A people can organise itself, but in the United States only Congress could create a territory and open a legal land system, and the settlers' code bound nobody outside the strip. In 1890 the strip was joined to the new Oklahoma Territory, and it became part of the state of Oklahoma.

The settlers wanted to join the country and asked to. The case shows the difference between land with no government and land outside the state. Their self-made code worked for a few years among neighbours, but it could not give them title that a court elsewhere would accept. Only the national government could do that, and it did so when it chose.

republic-of-cospaia.mechanism: A drafting error can produce real independence if both neighbours find it cheaper to tolerate than to fix, but those neighbours can end that tolerance by agreement.
republic-of-cospaia.story:
Cospaia was a tiny republic in northern Umbria, central Italy, that lasted nearly four centuries because of a mistake in a treaty. Today it is a hamlet of a few blocks in the comune of San Giustino, between the towns of Sansepolcro and Città di Castello.

In 1440 Pope Eugene IV, short of money during a struggle with the Council of Basel, handed the Sansepolcro district to Florence as security for a debt of 25,000 ducats. The treaty set the new border at a creek called the Rio. Two creeks with that name ran about 500 metres apart, and each side took the one nearer to itself. So 330 hectares around the village of Cospaia ended up belonging to neither. Its roughly 250 inhabitants declared themselves independent, with the Latin motto Perpetua et firma libertas, meaning lasting and firm liberty, which is still written over the church door.

In 1484 Florence and the Papal States accepted this, because they considered it not worth the trouble of redrawing the treaty. By local accounts the place had no taxes and no standing government. Goods passed through free of tariffs, and for a people between two taxing states that was the valuable part.

Tobacco reached the area in 1574. In 1624 a papal ban on it made the neighbouring Papal lands off limits, and Cospaia gave its farmland to the crop. The ponds for irrigating tobacco can still be seen.

The neighbours, by then Tuscany and the Papal States, complained of smugglers. On 25 May 1826 they agreed to divide the village, and the partition followed in June. Fourteen heads of families signed their submission in exchange for a silver coin each and permission to grow up to half a million tobacco plants a year.

Cospaia is one of the longest examples of a place existing through a neighbour's indifference, and it had real benefits for those who lived there. It lasted until complaints about smuggling made the two states want to change the arrangement, and they ended it by agreement.

republic-of-indian-stream.mechanism: A government set up in a disputed border area lasts only until one of the claiming powers is willing to use force. New Hampshire ended this one with a threat of militia occupation, without firing on it.
republic-of-indian-stream.story:
Indian Stream was a small self-governing republic from 1832 to 1835 in what is now the far north of New Hampshire, on the border with Canada. Its people did not want a new country for its own sake. They wanted to stop being taxed by two countries at once.

The 1783 treaty that ended the American Revolution set the border at the "northwesternmost head of the Connecticut River", and several streams could fit that description. Britain and the United States each claimed the land between them, and both sent in tax collectors and debt-collecting sheriffs. Settlers could be taxed or sued by either side.

To stop paying twice, about 300 settlers formed an assembly, declared independence on 9 July 1832 and wrote a constitution that was to last until the two powers settled the border. It set up an elected assembly and a Justice of the Peace, a post held by Luther Parker, one of the drafters. So they had built a temporary government with a stated end date, and they did not claim to be permanent.

The sheriff of Coos County, New Hampshire, kept acting there anyway. On 30 July 1835 he called for the militia, and two infantry companies gathered at nearby Stewartstown. On 4 August he met 30 to 40 assembly members and gave them an ultimatum, and most gave in. The next day five leaders told a British official that help had not come in time and that they had accepted annexation by New Hampshire. That shows the choice they faced, since their remaining hope was protection from the other claimant.

Trouble continued. That October an arrest over a hardware-store debt led armed locals to shoot a British deputy and capture a magistrate in Canada, and New Hampshire militia occupied the area until February 1836. The area became the town of Pittsburg in 1840, and the Webster-Ashburton Treaty of 1842 gave it to the United States.

The case shows how a small place can use a border dispute, and what limits it. While two powers both claim an area, neither is sure of its ground and a local government can exist between them. That ends when one claimant decides to use force and the other does not respond.

sapodilla-cayes.mechanism: Even tiny uninhabited land is rarely terra nullius (land belonging to no state). Any claim to it can end up in a case between states at the International Court of Justice.
sapodilla-cayes.story:
The Sapodilla Cayes are a small uninhabited atoll, a ring of tiny coral islands, in the Gulf of Honduras, run by Belize as a marine reserve. Nobody lives on them, yet three countries have an interest in them, and the dispute is now before the International Court of Justice, the United Nations' top court. They are included as a reminder that even a very small patch of empty land in the sea is unlikely to be free for anyone to claim.

Honduras claims the cayes in its 1982 constitution, and Guatemala claims the same territory in its separate case against Belize. On 16 November 2022 Belize took Honduras to the court, saying the cayes have been part of its territory since the early 19th century, first as the settlement of Belize, then as the colony of British Honduras, and since 1981 as an independent state. That is an argument from long government of the place, the kind international courts have rewarded in earlier island cases.

Guatemala applied on 1 December 2023 for permission to join the case, and hearings on that request ran from 24 to 26 November 2025. On 19 March 2026 the court unanimously allowed Guatemala to intervene as a non-party, meaning it can state its views without being bound as a full party, limited to the cayes and fishing rights around them. Fishing rights are part of what makes such small islands valuable. The court first set written filings for 20 July 2026, and an order of 16 April 2026 extended that deadline. The court has not yet ruled on who owns the cayes.

Anyone landing there with a flag would run into Belize's reserve rules first and a case involving three states after that.

floating-island-french-polynesia.mechanism: A special legal zone inside a state's waters needs that state's political consent. The memorandum here was not binding, so the government could walk away from it at no cost once locals objected.
floating-island-french-polynesia.story:
The Floating Island Project was a plan to build a floating settlement in a lagoon in French Polynesia, the self-governing French territory in the South Pacific that includes Tahiti. It came from the Seasteading Institute of San Francisco, a non-profit group that wants to create new societies on the ocean, with their own rules. It is the closest the seasteading movement has come to a government's agreement, and it shows how fragile that agreement was.

The institute chose French Polynesia for its links to France, its autonomy and its calm waters, and it said the idea had been started by Tahitians themselves. The project was also pitched as an answer to rising seas in low islands, with jobs and economic growth for the territory.

On 13 January 2017 French Polynesia signed a memorandum of understanding with the institute, a document that records intentions and is usually weaker than a contract. Minister Jean-Christophe Bouissou signed for the territory and executive director Randolph Hencken for the institute, and President Edouard Fritch appeared by video. The deal cleared the way for studies toward "seazones" with a special governing framework. The institute formed a company, Blue Frontiers, to build the project, which would also need legislation. It inspected sites near Tahiti, Tupai and Raiatea, and considered the Atimaono lagoon south of Tahiti for its depth and closeness to shore.

Local residents objected. Opposition politician Valentina Cross held up a protest poster and asked the government to withdraw, and the ruling Tapura Huiraatira party first said nothing had been signed. On 28 February 2018 RNZ, New Zealand's public broadcaster, reported the government's position that the deal had no legal force, had expired at the end of 2017, and was now void. No floating island was built, no one lived there and no court ever heard the matter.

A seazone would have depended entirely on one government's continuing will. It would sit in that government's waters, under law that government would have to pass, on behalf of a foreign group. The government lost nothing by withdrawing, because a memorandum binds no one, and the people who lived nearby had votes. The case shows that a group seeking a special zone has to win over local voters as well as ministers.

oceanix-busan.mechanism: Oceanix uses the same engineering idea as seasteading, floating land, but keeps it inside a country's territory with UN support. Building on the sea and leaving national law are separate things.
oceanix-busan.story:
Oceanix Busan is a proposed floating neighbourhood off Busan, a port city in South Korea, backed by the city government and UN-Habitat, the United Nations agency for cities. It is included as the opposite of the seasteading idea. The engineering is similar, with buildings on floating platforms, but it would stay under a city government and has no aim of leaving any state's law.

Its stated purpose is to give coastal cities new land as seas rise and housing costs grow. UN-Habitat said two of every five people live within 100 kilometres of a coast and that 90 percent of mega cities are vulnerable to rising seas. OCEANIX is a company based in New York, and the design was led by the architects Bjarke Ingels Group and SAMOO, part of the Samsung Group.

On 18 November 2021 Busan, UN-Habitat and OCEANIX signed an agreement to build a prototype, with about $200 million anticipated as the cost. On 26 April 2022, at UN Headquarters in New York, the three partners unveiled the design for what they called the world's first prototype sustainable floating city, and said they were on track to deliver it.

The practical advantage of working inside a country is that the hard questions have ready answers. South Korean law would apply to property, police and courts, and the city would be the partner for permits. The risks are the ordinary ones of any large building project, chiefly money. In October 2023 the Busan broadcaster KNN reported that a conference on the project gave no concrete financing or construction plans. Construction is not known to have started, no one is known to live there, and it is listed as not yet built.

seapods-panama.mechanism: After the Thai navy raid, the same promoters put their homes in a marina in a host country, accepting that country's law and permissions.
seapods-panama.story:
SeaPods are small floating homes built by the company Ocean Builders at Linton Bay Marina, in the province of Colón on the Caribbean coast of Panama. They are included because of how the company got there. Ocean Builders had first tried to live beyond national law and had come back inside one.

Its 2019 seastead off Phuket was raided by the Thai navy. Its 2020 plan to turn a cruise ship into a floating community, the MS Satoshi, collapsed because no insurer would cover it. It then turned to homes inside a state's waters, in a marina in a country that was willing to have them.

In September 2022 the Panamanian newspaper Panamá América reported houses being built in Colón, designed with the Dutch architect Koen Olthuis and his firm Waterstudio. The company took reservations for a $100 deposit, with prices from about $295,000 to $1.5 million. A SeaPod stands above the water on a float tethered to the seabed by anchors. It runs mainly on solar power, collects rain water and carries Starlink satellite internet and more than 100 sensors. The company's stated aim is to make the part of the world covered in water into a place to live.

At the unveiling on 22 September 2022, in front of an audience that included Panama's president, Laurentino Cortizo, the prototype tipped over with people inside. The company blamed a failed bilge pump, a pump that clears water from the hull, which it said upset the balance of a steel spar and caused flooding. It denied that the home sank, and AP reported no injuries. By June 2023 a Condé Nast Traveler writer stayed in one off Panama's Caribbean coast as among the first guests, and a Smithsonian researcher told the writer that floating pods touch the seabed less than bungalows on pillars.

The company does not claim independence from Panama, and Panamanian law applies to the marina. The number of permanent residents is not known. The case shows the most workable form of living on the water at present, which is a private home with a host government's permission and all of that government's law.

duran-sun.mechanism: A notary recording a claim only records that it was made, and a court accepting a consumer lawsuit only lets the case go ahead. Neither step makes a person the owner of a star.
duran-sun.story:
María Ángeles Durán, a woman from Vigo in Galicia, Spain, claims to own the Sun. Her case raises, in a simple form, the question of who the treaties on outer space bind.

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty says countries cannot claim a planet, a star or any other body in space as national territory. In 2010 Durán went to a notary and had her statement recorded that she owned the Sun. Her argument is that the treaty speaks of states and does not bind individuals. A notary's job is to confirm that a person appeared and made a statement, and it does not test whether the statement is true. She threatened to charge people for using solar power, and she sold plots on the Sun on the auction site eBay at one euro per square metre.

About two years after she opened her account, eBay removed the listings under its policy on intangible goods and blocked her account. According to Durán, eBay said the Sun "is not tangible and can't be sold", and she insisted it was a real product. She sued in court number 5 of Alcobendas, near Madrid, seeking 10,000 euros.

Reports differ on what the courts did next. A report from June 2015 said a Spanish court recognised her claim and let her pursue the dispute, with a first hearing set for 17 June 2015. The Mexican newspaper Excelsior said in 2022 that the court declared itself competent and gave her standing to sue, and it dated recognition of her ownership to 2012, without citing documents. The Spanish site Genbeta later wrote that the court dismissed her case and that a Spanish court said in 2016 that a person cannot legally own the Sun, but it names no court document and credits Excelsior, whose article does not say this.

Letting someone sue is a different thing from finding that she owns the Sun. A court can hear a dispute between a seller and a website without deciding whether the goods exist as property. No confirmed court ruling says she owns it. No one is known to have paid her for sunlight. Whether the treaty leaves room for private ownership is argued about by lawyers. To be real, though, ownership has to be backed by a state's courts and police, and the treaty bars states from claiming the land that would underpin such a title.

ad-coelum-downward.mechanism: Land ownership reaches downward only as far as the law allows, so anything dug beneath a plot stays part of the same property and the same country.
ad-coelum-downward.story:
Ad coelum is an old rule of property law about how far land ownership reaches up and down. The Latin phrase cuius est solum, eius est usque ad coelum et ad inferos means "whoever owns the soil, it is theirs all the way to the sky and to the depths". People who hope to leave national law by digging down often assume that a deep enough hole is somewhere new. This rule explains why it is not.

The saying has been traced to a note by the 13th-century Italian lawyer Accursius and is said to date in English law to the time of King Edward I. William Blackstone gave it its broad form in his Commentaries on the Laws of England in 1766, describing ownership as reaching upward and down to the centre of the earth. Largely through his influence the broad version shaped American law.

Modern law keeps only a limited version. Above the ground, an owner controls the space close to the land, so a neighbour's building cannot hang over it, but cannot stop flights far overhead. Below the ground, an owner holds rights to what is underneath, but in some places minerals beyond a set depth are separate from the land title. There the state often owns them permanently and leases them out for a fixed period. So what a buyer of land gets below ground depends on the local law, and it can be less than the old Latin saying suggests.

Suppose someone buys a plot and digs a chamber far below it. The rule settles who owns the chamber as against the neighbours. It says nothing about which country the chamber is in, since a country's territory includes what lies beneath its land. The owner holds the chamber under that country's law, and that country's planning rules, taxes and police apply. Owning down to the depths means owning within a state.

cyberbunker.mechanism: Calling a bunker a republic gives it no legal status. The country it stood in applied its licensing, wiretapping and criminal law to everything inside.
cyberbunker.story:
CyberBunker was a web-hosting business run from former military bunkers in the Netherlands and Germany, which called itself an independent republic. It hosted any website except those with child abuse material or terrorism, a service known as bulletproof hosting. Its customers in the 1990s were largely pornography sites, and it was later accused of hosting spammers, malware and online scams. It tested whether a thick concrete shell and a grand name could keep the law out.

In 1995 Herman-Johan Xennt bought a 20,000-square-foot former NATO bunker near Kloetinge in the south of the Netherlands, built in 1955 as a military command centre to survive a nuclear attack. Its spokesman, Sven Olaf Kamphuis, called it the Republic of CyberBunker and styled himself Minister of Telecommunications and Foreign Affairs. No state ever treated it as one.

The first failure came from an accident. In 2002 a fire brought emergency services inside, and they found a laboratory making the drug MDMA. Three men were jailed, and the town refused a business licence. That shows how ordinary local rules reach a so-called republic. The firm moved its servers above ground and kept advertising the bunker. In 2009 the file-sharing site The Pirate Bay moved to it, and a Hamburg court barred it from hosting the site in 2010. The ruling was aimed at the company operating in Germany as CB3Rob Ltd, which gave the court someone to order.

In 2011 and 2013 the anti-spam group Spamhaus blacklisted it. Shortly afterwards an attack that was then the largest publicly known of its kind, flooding targets with traffic, hit Spamhaus. Dutch prosecutors had Kamphuis arrested in Spain in 2013 over the attack. That shows the second limit. The people behind a claimed republic travel, and other countries can arrest them.

That year it bought a second bunker at Traben-Trarbach in Germany. Investigators tapped its traffic from 2015 and sent in undercover officers posing as a gardener and a cleaner. In September 2019, 600 police raided it. In late 2021 the regional court in Trier convicted all eight defendants, including Xennt, of belonging to a criminal organisation, but it did not convict them of aiding their customers' crimes. The difference shows how the prosecution succeeded, since membership of a criminal organisation could be proved where help with a customer's particular crime was not. Sentences ran from one suspended year to five years and nine months. In 2023 Germany's Federal Court of Justice largely upheld the verdict.

The bunker was built to resist bombs. The case ended with police, warrants and a court of the country it stood in.

pionen-bahnhof.mechanism: A hardened site protects servers from physical harm. Its legal protection comes entirely from the law of the country it stands in.
pionen-bahnhof.story:
Pionen is a data centre, a building full of computer servers, inside a former wartime shelter under the city of Stockholm, Sweden. The shelter was built in 1943 in the White Mountains in the Södermalm district to protect government functions in wartime. The Swedish internet provider Bahnhof converted it, and it opened on 11 September 2008.

It lies under 30 metres of granite, behind a door 40 centimetres thick, can be reached only by an entrance tunnel, and is described as able to withstand a hydrogen bomb. It covers 1,100 square metres and has greenhouses, fountains, simulated daylight and a large saltwater fish tank. Its two backup generators are submarine engines. Bahnhof also rents space there to others, and in 2010 the document-leaking organisation WikiLeaks kept servers on the site.

The case is included as a contrast. People who want their data safe often mix up two kinds of safety. One is protection from physical harm, and rock and steel provide that. The other is protection from a government's orders, and only law provides that. HavenCo, a company on the self-declared sea fort of Sealand, sold a similar hardened home for data, and it relied on a claim of independence. Pionen makes no such claim. It stands at Renstiernas gata 35 and 37 in central Stockholm, and Swedish government and law apply to it as to any other business. A Swedish court order would reach it as readily as an office above ground.

survival-condo.mechanism: Buying a missile silo gives ordinary ownership of land in Kansas, so debts, lawsuits and courts reach the bunker as they reach any other property.
survival-condo.story:
Survival Condo is a luxury underground bunker for rich people preparing for disaster, built inside an old missile silo in Kansas. It is included because it is one of the most fortified private homes in the world, and the law still reached it through an unpaid loan.

In 2008 Larry Hall bought a disused one, Raven Ridge 11 near Concordia, for $300,000. It goes down 197 feet. He built a 15-floor bunker with 12 condominium units for up to 75 people, plus a swimming pool, theatre, library, gym, climbing wall, vegetable gardens, fish tanks and three years of stored food. It also has armouries, a sniper post with a remote-controlled rifle and a jail cell. Building finished by 2012 at a cost of about $20 million.

Hall said all units had sold by 2017, though 6 appeared for sale in 2020, and no owners were living there that year. It works as a condominium, a kind of shared ownership in which people own their units and share the common parts. The facility is owned by a Kansas not-for-profit company, Raven Ridge of Kansas Site 11, Inc., incorporated in 2012. Hall has also discussed a second silo about 25 miles away, and he held options on four others in 2017.

Ordinary law applied to it as it does anywhere. Peter Ziegler, who bought Unit 5 in 2013, lent Hall's company $3 million, due a year later. After he died in 2017, his estate demanded the money, sued in January 2019, saying assets had been moved to other companies, and the two sides settled that August.

Their units are ordinary real estate, subject to county records, company law, courts and creditors.

unclos-shelf-subsoil.mechanism: Beyond the territorial sea, the rock under the continental shelf stays under the coastal country's exclusive control, including by tunnel, even where the water above is free to all.
unclos-shelf-subsoil.story:
The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), the main treaty on the oceans, sets out who controls the rock under the sea near a country's coast. It was concluded in 1982. It matters to anyone who thinks that going under the sea floor, far from shore, would take them beyond any state. The rules are in Part VI of the treaty, on the continental shelf, the shallow sea floor that extends from a country's land.

Start with the zones. Close to shore is the territorial sea, a belt of water a country fully controls. Article 76 defines the shelf as the seabed and subsoil beyond that belt. It runs out to the edge of the continental margin, or to 200 nautical miles from the coast where the margin stops short.

Article 77 gives the coastal country sovereign rights to explore the shelf and take its natural resources, including minerals in the subsoil. These rights are exclusive, so if the country leaves them unused, nobody else may use them without its express consent.

Article 85 adds that nothing in this part limits a coastal country's right to exploit the subsoil by tunnelling, however deep the water above. This means a country can run a tunnel out from its own shore under the sea. Article 78 says these rights do not change the status of the water above, which can be open to all ships. So a ship may sail freely over a spot where it may not drill. Article 80 applies the treaty's rule on artificial islands to the shelf as well, so structures fixed to the shelf fall within the same coastal rights.

Suppose a group anchors a ship 150 miles off a coast and sinks a shaft into the rock below. They are in international waters as far as the ship goes, and on the coastal country's shelf as far as the shaft goes. They would need that country's express consent to take anything from the subsoil. Past the end of the shelf, the deep ocean floor and its subsoil fall under other parts of the treaty. So the rock under the sea near coasts is not unclaimed space, even where the sea above it is open.

vivos-shelters.mechanism: Vivos sells underground space as ordinary property, so German fire codes and US geological reviews apply to it as they would to any building above ground.
vivos-shelters.story:
Vivos is a California company, founded by Robert Vicino, that sells places in underground shelters for use after a disaster. It treats underground space as a product, which is why it belongs with the cases on digging down. Its buyers get a private contract and no separate legal status.

Its first completed shelter, in Indiana, dates from the Cold War, was built to withstand a near direct hit from a 20-megaton bomb, and holds 80 people. In 2016 the company took over shelters built in 1967 at the former Black Hills Ordnance Depot in South Dakota, where it lists 575 bunkers of about 2,150 square feet each. It also planned to convert a Soviet-built complex at Rothenstein in Germany for 1,000 people, where fire rules were expected to require sprinklers throughout.

In 2013 Vivos acquired rights to buy part of a former limestone mine at Atchison, Kansas, once owned by the US Army, for 5,000 people. It cancelled that in June 2014 after Army geologists raised concerns about collapses. In September 2022 Vicino said the firm had about 100,000 members and over 1,000 buyers, figures that come from the company.

These episodes show the plain position of such a project. A German fire code and an American geological review applied just as they would to a hotel or a mine above ground, and the shelters would stay on land under US or German law.

aquarius-reef-base.why: Added that FIU took ownership in October 2014, per Wikipedia. The 2013 date for operations is kept from the entry.
aquarius-reef-base.mechanism: Aquarius shows the usual arrangement for undersea habitats. They are placed in a coastal country's managed waters and run under its authority, with no claim to the seabed.
aquarius-reef-base.story:
Aquarius is an underwater research laboratory on the sea floor off Florida, where scientists live for days at a time. It sits 62 feet down next to Conch Reef, 5.4 miles off Key Largo, in the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, a protected area run by the US government. It holds four scientists and two technicians on missions that average about ten days.

Its importance lies in how people can stay down so long. Divers normally have to come up slowly to let gases leave their bodies. Aquarius crews use saturation diving. After staying under pressure, their bodies reach a steady state, so they can work outside for up to nine hours a day and need to decompress only once, at the end of the mission. People who live at depth this way are called aquanauts. Research has ranged from coral disease to the way nutrients move through the reef, and NASA uses the base to train astronauts for spacewalks and lunar missions.

The habitat was built in Victoria, Texas, in 1986 and was first named after George Bond, the Navy doctor behind the SEALAB experiments. It first worked in the US Virgin Islands and was placed in the Keys in 1993. It was owned by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the US ocean agency. Florida International University took over operations in 2013 and then ownership in October 2014.

Until 2026, reporters described it as the only undersea research laboratory in operation. Living on the sea floor changed nothing legally. Its permissions come from the US government that manages the sanctuary. It has never been the basis for any claim to the seabed below it, and it continues to operate. For anyone imagining a home on the sea floor as a place outside the law, the longest-running example is a university laboratory in a federally managed sanctuary.

aquatica-chamberland.mechanism: A permanent colony on a seabed within divers' reach would be on a coastal country's continental shelf, where that country has exclusive rights over the bottom and its resources. The plan named no way around this.
aquatica-chamberland.story:
Aquatica was a proposal for a permanent human settlement on the sea floor, put forward by Dennis Chamberland, an aquanaut (a person who lives under water for long stretches) and bioengineer with thirty years at NASA. He described it as the first underwater settlement meant for permanent colonization, and spoke of children born under water, with schools and hospitals.

He had real experience. He had commanded seven NASA underwater missions, grown crops in controlled settings on the ocean floor, and built a two-person habitat off Key Largo, Florida, that the film director James Cameron visited. The first step, reported in February 2011, was to be a four-person underwater house called Leviathan, expected to be lowered to the seabed the following year. Its stated purpose was for residents to monitor and protect the ocean.

The report gave no site, budget or legal basis, and Leviathan is not known to have been placed. The legal question would have been waiting. Any seabed divers can reach from a shore base would most likely be on some country's continental shelf, the shallow sea floor off its coast, where under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea that country keeps exclusive rights over the bottom and its resources. A family living there would still need a country's law for birth records, schooling and medical care, and the plan did not say which.

conshelf-precontinent.mechanism: Cousteau's stations showed that people could live on the continental shelf for a month, but they depended on supplies from the surface, and the commercial reason to pay for a permanent colony went away.
conshelf-precontinent.story:
Conshelf, also called Précontinent, was a series of three experiments in the 1960s by the French ocean explorer Jacques Cousteau and his team to build an underwater village, going deeper each time. The name is short for continental shelf station. The continental shelf is the shallow sea floor along a coast,. Part of the money came from the French petrochemical industry, which hoped such colonies could serve as bases for exploiting the sea.

Conshelf One, in 1962, put two divers in a small chamber 12 metres down off Marseille for two weeks. In 1963 Conshelf Two placed six oceanauts in a starfish-shaped house 10 metres down at Sha'ab Rumi in the Red Sea off Sudan, for 30 days. A hangar held a small two-person submarine, and two more men lived for a week in a "deep cabin" at 30 metres.

The village depended entirely on the surface. Air, water, food and power all came from a large team on the surface and two support ships. Cousteau's film of it, World Without Sun, won an Academy Award in the documentary category.

Conshelf Three followed a few years later. Cousteau then withdrew his support for this kind of use of the sea and turned to conservation. Later work showed that robots and divers sent from the surface could do industrial jobs more efficiently, so companies had no need for people living on the bottom. Parts of Conshelf Two remain on the sea floor and are visited by recreational divers.

The experiments proved that people could live on the shelf for a month. They did not create any legal status, and they make clear what ended the idea. The money had come from an expected commercial use, and that use disappeared.

deep-vanguard-sentinel.mechanism: A private undersea habitat on the continental shelf falls under the coastal country's rights over that shelf, so moving a module means needing a different country's permission.
deep-vanguard-sentinel.story:
DEEP is a private UK-based company building undersea habitats where people could live and work on the sea floor. Its prototype, Vanguard, was installed in the Florida Keys in June 2026, according to the Miami Herald via the radio station WLRN, which made it the Keys' second undersea habitat and a privately funded one. The company's director of scientific research, Dawn Kernagis, said it had been over 40 years since a new human undersea habitat was launched.

Vanguard sits at Tennessee Reef in the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, a protected area run by the US government, in 17 metres of water. It is designed for up to four people on missions of five days or more. Earlier plans gave three people at 100 metres. At the end of June 2026 it was still in sea testing and commissioning, working toward classification by DNV, a body that certifies ships and marine equipment, with crew training and first missions to follow.

It is the first step toward a larger system called Sentinel, planned for 2027. Sentinel's modules would hold six people each, up to 50 in all, join into a larger complex and let people stay at 200 metres for 28 days, on the continental shelf, the shallow sea floor off a coast. Boat International reported it might go to the Mediterranean.

Because the modules can be moved and redeployed, a different country's permission would apply at each site, since the coastal country holds the rights over its shelf. DEEP makes no claim to sovereignty, and press coverage describes science and industry uses and no attempt to gain independence from the host country. No crew had been reported living in it at the time of those reports.

jules-undersea-lodge.mechanism: A habitat in a lagoon on Florida property is simply a building under water, so state and federal law apply to it as they do on the shore.
jules-undersea-lodge.story:
Jules' Undersea Lodge is a small underwater habitat in a lagoon at Key Largo, Florida, where visitors can stay overnight. It began in the 1970s as La Chalupa, a working research laboratory in Puerto Rico used to keep scientists under pressure for long stays, a method called saturation diving. It was later moved to Key Largo, and as Jules' Undersea Lodge, it gave thousands of divers the experience of sleeping beneath the sea.

Its operator today, MarineLab Undersea Park & Museum, calls it Jules' Undersea Lab. Guided dives tour it, and visitors can spend 24 hours inside on what the park calls an Aquanaut Mission. Universities and research teams can use it for diving medicine, training for space missions and marine science. The park also keeps the old MarineLab Undersea Laboratory on land as a museum piece, along with an exhibit on Ian Koblick.

It operates as a public attraction in a protected lagoon, with a dock, a gift shop and advance bookings, on the shore of a US state, and it makes no claim to independence. It is a reminder that a person can sleep under water without having left anywhere, because the lagoon is part of Florida.

ocean-spiral.mechanism: Ocean Spiral assumes government funding and makes no claim to independence, which shows that plans for undersea cities do not have to involve leaving a state's control.
ocean-spiral.story:
Ocean Spiral is a design for an underwater city published in November 2014 by Shimizu Corporation, a Japanese construction company. It was reported in the trade press with a central section called the Blue Garden. The plan described a 75-storey colony housing 5,000 people in linked spheres, with over 1,000 homes, a 400-room hotel and 50,000 square metres of offices. Each watertight sphere would be attached to the ocean floor and could sink below the surface in bad weather.

Power would come from micro-organism factories producing methane, and drinking water from removing salt from seawater. Shimizu expected the needed technology by 2030, followed by five more years of building, at a cost of ¥3 trillion, about US$25 billion. It expected Japan's government and private investors to help pay.

The design says nothing about leaving any national law and names no site, so the marker sits in Japan, the company's home country, and nothing has been built. It is included to show that a company can imagine a full undersea city entirely as a building project paid for partly by a state. In that form it would need the state's permission, and it would have to comply with that state's rules.

proteus-curacao.mechanism: Proteus would be built in one island's waters by agreement with its government, the usual legal pattern for undersea stations, with no attempt to create a new jurisdiction.
proteus-curacao.story:
Proteus is a planned undersea research station off the Caribbean island of Curaçao, proposed by Fabien Cousteau, grandson of the explorer Jacques Cousteau, through his company Proteus Ocean Group. He decided to build it after spending 31 days in the Aquarius undersea laboratory off Florida in 2014, and he describes it as a space station for the sea. It first reached the press in August 2020.

The main living spaces would be about 20 metres down, inside a marine park off the island's northeast coast, with a deeper satellite module at 70 metres. It is modular, meaning built from connected units, and could hold 12 people normally and up to 18 at a squeeze.

Money is the main obstacle. Dive magazine reported that it needed US$60 million to build and US$75 million to run for its first three years, paid for by renting space to technology firms and research centres. Curaçao's prime minister, Gilmar Pisas, announced that it was expected to be finished in 2026 near Fuik. A Boat International report in October 2024 said it was still in planning, with launch hoped for around 2027 and heavy funding still needed. An expert quoted there said going under water is very costly and has been harder to achieve than reaching the moon. It is not known to have been built.

It would sit in Curaçao's waters with the government's backing, and no one has claimed sovereignty over the seabed or the water above. That is the usual pattern for undersea stations. The host government gives permission and support.

sealab.mechanism: Living on the sea floor for weeks gave the navy data on saturation diving and no legal claim to the bottom. It was a government experiment that needed a surface ship throughout.
sealab.story:
SEALAB was a US Navy programme in the 1960s to test whether people could live under pressure on the sea floor for long periods, a method called saturation diving. Captain George Bond, a Navy doctor, had worked on the theory since 1957. Divers who stay at depth absorb gases until their bodies can hold no more, so they need one long decompression at the end of the stay and not one after each dive.

SEALAB I went down off Bermuda on 20 July 1964 to 192 feet, with four divers planning a three-week stay. It was built from two converted floats and held in place with axles from railroad cars. It showed that saturation diving in the open ocean could work for long periods. SEALAB II followed in 1965 in the La Jolla Canyon off California. It was nearly twice the size, with heating coils to fight the chill caused by breathing helium, along with hot showers and a toilet. Teams stayed 15 days, and the former astronaut Scott Carpenter stayed a record 30, with 28 divers in all. They tested tools and salvage methods.

SEALAB III came four years later, 18 months late and $3 million over budget. It was lowered to 610 feet off San Clemente Island on 15 February 1969. When a seal leaked helium, divers who had been awake for twenty hours went down to repair it, and the aquanaut Berry Cannon died on the second attempt. A Navy inquiry found that his breathing equipment lacked the chemical that removes carbon dioxide, while a 2024 study by an ocean engineer pointed to electrocution. Because of his death the programme was halted, and no new habitat was built.

SEALAB has a simple place in the legal picture. It was run by a government navy with a surface ship in support throughout, so nobody asked who governed it. The experiments created knowledge about diving and no claim to any seabed. It also shows the physical risk of living at such depths, which any private group would have to carry without a navy behind it.

northern-cyprus.mechanism: A UN Security Council call not to recognise a territory can keep it out of the international system for decades, while one supporting state keeps it running in practice.
northern-cyprus.story:
Northern Cyprus is a self-declared state covering the northern third of the Mediterranean island of Cyprus, recognised as a country only by Turkey. It holds elections, has a president and a 50-member assembly, and has run itself for decades. It is the clearest example of a place with a government that the rest of the world has been told not to recognise.

Cyprus became independent from Britain in 1960 under a constitution that shared power between its Greek and Turkish communities, but violence between them soon followed. Many Greek Cypriots wanted enosis, union with Greece, and many Turkish Cypriots wanted the island partitioned. In 1974 a coup backed by Greece's military government, seeking to annex the island, prompted Turkey to invade and capture the north. Much of the Greek Cypriot population in the north was evicted, and Turkish Cypriots fled from the south. A 1975 agreement in Vienna arranged a population exchange.

In 1983 the north declared independence without agreement from the Republic of Cyprus, as the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus. Resolution 541 of the UN Security Council, the UN's top body on peace and war, rejected the declaration as legally invalid and urged UN members not to recognise it. Other countries were asked to withhold acceptance even though the north held territory and ran a government. Other countries treat the area as Republic of Cyprus territory under Turkish military occupation.

Non-recognition has practical effects on everyday life. The Republic of Cyprus, as the recognised authority, has declared the north's airports and ports closed, so an international embargo applies, and trade goes through Turkey. The north uses the Turkish lira, which ties its economy to Turkey's. Because of this isolation it relies on Turkey for economic, political and military support. Some experts call it a puppet state, while others dispute that because of its separate elections and government.

A UN settlement known as the Annan Plan went to a referendum in April 2004. Turkish Cypriots supported it, and the plan failed, so the division continues. The European Union, having admitted Cyprus as a member, pledged to end the north's isolation, and those pledges lost momentum. A UN buffer zone still divides the island, and Tufan Erhürman is the north's current president.

The case shows the weight of a Security Council call. Territory, people and a working government did not bring recognition, and one powerful supporter was enough to keep the place going without it.

republic-of-artsakh.mechanism: A place that governs itself without recognition has no international protection, and the state that holds recognised title to the land may take it back by force.
republic-of-artsakh.story:
Artsakh, also called Nagorno-Karabakh, was a breakaway state of ethnic Armenians inside the internationally recognised borders of Azerbaijan, in the South Caucasus, with its capital at Stepanakert. It lasted 32 years. It is the plainest modern example of what can happen to an unrecognised state when the country it broke away from becomes strong enough to take it back.

In Soviet times the region was a self-governing area within Soviet Azerbaijan, with an Armenian majority. From 1988 its Armenians campaigned to join Armenia, citing fears for their culture and safety under Azerbaijani rule, which led to violence. As the Soviet Union collapsed, Azerbaijan declared independence and on 27 November 1991 cancelled the region's autonomy, and the region voted for independence that December. Azerbaijan rejected the declaration, and full-scale war followed. It ended with a ceasefire in May 1994 that left Armenian forces in control of the region and much of the surrounding land.

From then on Artsakh ran its own president, parliament and elections, relying on Armenia for money and military support, although Armenia never formally recognised it. No UN member did. The European Union, the United States and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation rejected its elections. Other governments treated the territory as part of Azerbaijan throughout. The two armies faced each other across a contested line, with deadly incidents over the years.

In a new war in 2020 Azerbaijan retook the surrounding districts and much of Artsakh's land, leaving it an enclave linked to Armenia only by the Lachin corridor, a road watched by Russian peacekeepers. In December 2022 Azerbaijanis blocked that road, causing a humanitarian crisis. In September 2023 Azerbaijan attacked and took the remaining land, and almost the entire population left for Armenia within days, in what is widely described as an effective expulsion.

On 28 September 2023 President Samvel Shahramanyan signed a decree dissolving all state institutions by 1 January 2024, although he later tried to cancel it. Azerbaijan now controls the territory. Thirty-two years of elections and institutions gave Artsakh no legal protection, because other governments had always treated the land as Azerbaijan's.

rojava.mechanism: This self-rule, won during a civil war, lasted while the central government was weak and foreign backers stayed involved. It ended through a military offensive and a negotiated merger into the Syrian state.
rojava.story:
The Autonomous Administration of North and East Syria, also called Rojava, was a Kurdish-led self-governing region in north-eastern Syria that lasted from 2012 to 2026. It never asked to be an independent country. It sought self-rule inside Syria, and it shows how such a place can arise in a civil war and how it can end when the war does.

Many of Syria's Kurds were stateless. In 2011, as the uprising began, President Bashar al-Assad granted about 220,000 Kurds citizenship. In 2012 Kurdish-led forces took control of parts of the north-east in practice. Their main party, the PYD, drew on the ideas of Abdullah Öcalan, leader of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK), a militant Kurdish group. In March 2016 Kurdish groups announced a federal system, and a constitution followed that December. In September 2018 the region took its later name and was organised into sub-regions that at various times included Afrin, Jazira, Euphrates, Raqqa, Tabqa, Manbij and Deir ez-Zor.

Its armed force was the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). It ran some foreign relations but was not recognised as autonomous by Syria or by any other state, although the Parliament of Catalonia, a regional body in Spain, did recognise it.

Its survival rested on the balance of forces around it. From 2016 Turkish forces and Turkish-backed Syrian rebels occupied parts of northern Syria in a series of operations. In January 2026 Syria's transitional government took back those areas and launched an offensive in the north-east, capturing up to 80 percent of the administration's land, and the rest was handed over under an agreement to merge it into the Syrian state.

On 20 August 2026 SDF commander Mazloum Abdi said the military, security and administrative bodies had been integrated. After an agreement with President Ahmed al-Sharaa, he announced the SDF's dissolution on 25 August, and Syrian state television said this also covered the autonomous administration. The number of people under its rule is not known. The case shows that self-rule won while a central government is weak does not, on its own, turn into a legal right once that government recovers.

somaliland.mechanism: A place can meet the practical tests of statehood for decades (people, land, government, foreign contacts) and still lack recognition, because recognition is a political decision made by other states.
somaliland.story:
Somaliland is a self-declared state in the Horn of Africa, on the Gulf of Aden, which has governed itself since 1991 while Somalia still claims it as its own. It covers 176,120 square kilometres and has about 6.2 million people. Its capital is Hargeisa. It is the leading example of a place that seems to meet the practical tests of statehood and still lacks wide recognition.

It was a British protectorate that united with Somalia in 1960, but the constitution put to a referendum in 1961 had little support in the north. Harsh policies against the Isaaq clan under Somalia's president Siad Barre led to a 10-year war. It ended with a declaration of independence in 1991, agreed at a large conference in Burao, as Somalia fell into civil war.

Since then Somaliland has held its own elections, run its own government and issued its own currency, the Somaliland shilling. Its parliament includes an upper House of Elders.
