It issues passports, and South Africa is reported to accept them. The New York Times reported that it has governed most of the land it claims largely in peace and stability. It belongs to the Unrepresented Nations and Peoples Organization, an advocacy group for those without a seat at the UN.

Statehood has usual tests, which are people, a defined territory, a government and the ability to deal with other states. Somaliland can point to all of them. Recognition, meaning other states accepting a place as a state, is a separate decision that each government takes for its own reasons. For decades none did so. Somaliland kept informal ties and hosted offices from Ethiopia and Taiwan. Taiwan and Somaliland signed a cooperation agreement in 2020 and exchanged offices, and whether they recognise each other is unclear.

On 26 December 2025 Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu signed an agreement recognising it as an independent and sovereign state, making Israel the first UN member to do so. Several governments objected, among them Algeria and Azerbaijan, which said the step violated Somalia's sovereignty and unity. As of October 2026 Israel remained the only one. According to The New York Times, other governments fear recognition could encourage secession elsewhere.

The case shows the limits of building a state from within. Decades of order and elections have brought Somaliland contacts and one recognition. Wider recognition depends on the decisions of other governments.

taiwan.mechanism: Effective government and a large population do not guarantee recognition, because other states decide it, and here they must also weigh a rival government that claims the same territory.
taiwan.story:
Taiwan is an island off the coast of China that has its own government and elections, but few countries formally recognise it as a state. Its government, the Republic of China (ROC), controls Taiwan and nearby islands, 36,193 square kilometres with about 23.3 million people. Its case shows that size and success do not settle recognition.

The ROC once governed mainland China. It retreated to Taiwan on 7 December 1949 as the Communist Party won the civil war and founded the People's Republic of China (PRC). For decades two governments each claimed to be the one government of all China. The ROC was a founding member of the United Nations, but in 1971 UN members voted that the PRC, the government in Beijing, was China's rightful representative. That vote concerned who speaks for China, and it removed Taiwan's government from the UN.

Taiwan then changed from within. In the late 1980s and early 1990s it moved from a one-party state under martial law to a multi-party democracy. The ROC kept claiming to be the sole government of all China until 1991, when it stopped treating the Communist Party as a rebel group and accepted that the Party controlled the mainland. It has its own constitution and courts, and rapid industrial growth began in the 1960s.

The PRC claims Taiwan and refuses diplomatic relations with any country that recognises the ROC, so other states have to choose. Most choose Beijing. Taiwan now has formal relations with only 11 of the 193 UN members and the Holy See. Its foreign ministry lists them, among them Paraguay, Guatemala, Belize, Eswatini and Palau. Many other countries keep unofficial ties.

This differs from most breakaway cases, because Taiwan faces a rival government claiming the same territory and other states must pick between the two. Beijing says Taiwan is part of China, and Taiwan continues to govern itself. For someone thinking of founding a territory, the figures give the scale of the problem. About 23 million people with a working state still depend on other governments' choices for their standing.

transnistria.mechanism: Military backing can keep an unrecognised territory in place for decades. Its citizens get around non-recognition by also carrying the passport of a recognised country.
transnistria.story:
Transnistria is a breakaway territory in a narrow strip of land east of the Dniester river, legally part of Moldova, which no UN member recognises as a country. Not even Russia, which keeps soldiers there, does so. Its capital is Tiraspol. It shows how long an unrecognised place can last when a stronger country's troops stand behind it.

On 2 September 1990, as the Soviet Union was falling apart, a local assembly proclaimed a separate Soviet republic there, amid fears that Moldova would reunite with Romania. A war in 1992 killed about 1,000 people, and Russian troops already stationed there intervened on the separatists' side. The ceasefire set up a joint control commission of Moldova, Russia and Transnistria and a peacekeeping force under it. The ceasefire has held. Talks in a format called 5+2, started in 2005 and involving Moldova, Transnistria, Russia, Ukraine and the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe with the US and EU as observers, have not produced a settlement.

Transnistria runs its own government, parliament, army, police, post office and vehicle plates. Its central bank issues the Transnistrian ruble, which can be exchanged only inside the territory,. Its population fell from 555,347 in 2004 to 475,373 in 2015. Its own citizenship papers are not accepted abroad, so many residents hold Moldovan citizenship, and many also hold Russian, Romanian or Ukrainian passports. Those passports are how residents travel abroad.

The territory depends on its neighbours. After Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, Ukraine sealed its border with Transnistria, which had been the main route for goods, so it became wholly reliant on Moldova to let imports through. On 1 January 2025 the deal that delivered Russian gas through Ukraine ended, halting the flow of gas and creating a severe energy crisis. An agreement in August 2025 addressed the gas flow.

Rights inside are limited too, as Deutsche Welle has reported. A resident told it he was arrested four times for disrespecting state order. On 4 September 2024 its parliament banned public use of the name Transnistria, with a fine or up to 15 days in jail as the penalty. The case shows that being outside a recognised state does not by itself bring more freedom for residents.

wa-state.mechanism: An armed group can give up its claim to independence in exchange for near-total self-rule under a peace deal, while relying on a neighbouring country's economy for money and services.
wa-state.story:
Wa State is a self-governing region of about 30,000 square kilometres in Shan State in north-eastern Myanmar, on the border with China, that runs its own affairs with its own army. Its capital is Pangkham. It is an unusual case because it does not claim to be a country. It accepts Myanmar's sovereignty on paper and in practice is run as a separate state.

In April 1989 Wa fighters led by Bao Youxiang split from the Communist Party of Burma, which had been fighting the government, and formed the United Wa State Party and its army. On 9 May 1989 they signed a ceasefire with the central government. In return for stopping fighting, they were given land to run as they wished. That ceasefire has held since.

They grew poppies, and in the following decade the region became one of the world's leading producers of opium and heroin. From 1999 to 2002, 80,000 former opium farmers were forcibly moved to more fertile land in the south, and some groups report that thousands died.

Day to day it looks more like China than Myanmar. The ruling party copies China's political system, with a Politburo and a people's congress, and has its own administrative divisions and army. The money is the Chinese yuan, the main language is Mandarin, and electricity and mobile networks come from Chinese companies. The BBC's Jonah Fisher visited in 2016 and reported that Google Maps did not show it and that visa requests were refused. He said the region had schools and infrastructure, partly built with illicit money.

Legally, it accepts Myanmar's sovereignty over its territory but gives no allegiance to any specific government, and Myanmar's 2008 constitution recognises the northern part as a self-administered area. When fighting grew in northern Shan State in 2023, the Wa stayed neutral, and the region remains outside the central government's control.

The case shows that a declaration of independence is not the only route to self-rule. By giving up the claim, the Wa leaders avoided the question of recognition altogether. Their position rests on their own army, their neighbour's economy and the ceasefire.

landis-venus-aerostats.mechanism: The Outer Space Treaty's Article II bars any country from taking a planet by use or occupation. Whether a city drifting in the air counts is an open question, because it occupies no fixed ground and the treaty does not address this directly.
landis-venus-aerostats.story:
Geoffrey Landis, a scientist at NASA's Glenn Research Center in Ohio, proposed that people could live in floating cities in the clouds of Venus. He presented his paper, Colonization of Venus, at a conference on human space exploration in Albuquerque in February 2003.

The surface of Venus is far too hot and crushing for people, with a ground pressure about 91 times the pressure of Earth's air. Landis argued that the only trouble is that the ground lies too far below the level where pressure is comfortable, so settlers should live in the air. At about 50 kilometres up, pressure is close to that at sea level on Earth and the temperature is 0 to 50 C. An aerostat, a craft that floats like a balloon, could use ordinary breathable air as its lifting gas, because air is lighter than the carbon dioxide around it. So the living space itself would hold the city up. Landis's figure is over 60% of helium's lifting power on Earth.

He worked through what daily life would mean. People going outside would need breathable air and protection from acid and some heat, but no pressure suit. Because pressure inside and outside would be about equal, a leak would mix slowly, leaving time for repairs. The structures would have to resist sulfuric acid in the clouds, and the atmosphere above would shield against radiation as well as Earth's does. At the far extreme, aerostats might cover the whole planet.

Nothing has been built, and the idea remains a paper proposal. The legal question is untested. Article II of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty bars any country from taking a planet by claim, use or occupation. A city drifting in the air occupies no fixed ground, and the treaty does not address this directly. Whether anyone could claim the air around it has never been decided.

nasa-havoc.mechanism: A government study makes no claim to territory, and because HAVOC never went forward, its permanent phase was never tested against the Outer Space Treaty's ban on any country taking a planet or other body in space.
nasa-havoc.story:
HAVOC, short for High Altitude Venus Operational Concept, was a NASA study of how people could explore Venus from airships floating high in its atmosphere. It was created in 2014 by Dale Arney and Chris Jones, engineers in the Space Mission Analysis Branch at NASA's Langley Research Center in Virginia, after a meeting about living on Mars prompted the idea. They published it at an American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics conference in Pasadena in 2015.

The plan targeted 55 kilometres above Venus, where the temperature is 27 C and the pressure about half that at sea level on Earth. It ran in five phases. A robot airship 31 metres long would go first, then astronauts in orbit around Venus, then a crew staying about 30 days in an airship 129 metres long. After that would come a one-year stay, and finally a permanent human presence in the atmosphere. Travel out would take 110 days and return 300, for 440 days in total, so even the short mission meant more than a year away from Earth.

NASA later said HAVOC was an internal study for building analysis skills and never a real mission for human exploration. It received no further funding and was cancelled by 2017, though some of its technologies were developed further for possible Moon and Mars missions.

As a government study it made no claim to any territory. Its last phase would have raised a question that has never been tested. The 1967 Outer Space Treaty bans any country from taking a planet or other body in space, and the treaty does not say how that applies to a permanent crew floating in a planet's air. Because HAVOC stopped at the study stage, it never had to be answered.

zhitomirsky-floating-islands.mechanism: This was a design proposal with no reported claim of ownership, made before the Moon Agreement, a later treaty on the Moon and other bodies in the solar system.
zhitomirsky-floating-islands.story:
The Floating Islands of Venus was a 1971 proposal by the Soviet engineer and science fiction writer Sergei Zhitomirsky for cities floating in the atmosphere of Venus, high above its hostile surface. He thought the technology used in zeppelins and hot air balloons could keep stations afloat some 50 or 60 kilometres above the surface, where temperature and other conditions were thought to be comfortable for people.

It is an early version of the idea, and Soviet scientists were suggesting settlement of the Venusian atmosphere at least as early as 1971. In 1991 Paul Birch suggested a related design, two-part domes filled with hydrogen or helium, in the Journal of the British Interplanetary Society. None of these was built. He is not known to have claimed ownership of any part of Venus. It came four years after the 1967 Outer Space Treaty barred countries from claiming planets, and before the Moon Agreement, a later treaty on the Moon and other bodies in the solar system.
